items.title: After my husband was diagnosed with colon cancer at 45, we changed our family diet. Here's what we eat — and don't eat — now.
items.summary: The author's husband was diagnosed with colon cancer at 45. Courtesy of Lindsay Karp My husband, 45, is a doctor and encourages his patients to get routine colonoscopies on time. When he went in for his own, he was surprised to be diagnosed with colon cancer. He had no symptoms. Now, we're changing our diets, and what our kids eat, as well. When my husband, a doctor, went in for his first routine colonoscopy at 45 years old, he said nonchalantly, "I'll be done by noon. Then we can grab lunch." He recommends that his patients be screened on time, so he was simply following his own advice. He had no symptoms suggesting anything was wrong, so when they found a few polyps — the largest one measuring 55 millimeters — we were caught off guard. A second procedure was necessary to remove the larger polyp, and when the biopsy came back showing cancer, our lives crumbled in an instant. The right portion of his colon was removed, and three weeks later, our whirlwind nightmare began to settle. Luckily, having his screening on time saved his life. Now, we're focused on preventive care . We're changing our diets, and what our kids eat, too An average person has about a 4% to 5% lifetime chance of developing colorectal cancer — but having one affected parent raises that risk to roughly 5% to 15%. Someone with a first-degree relative who had colon cancer should have their first screening at 40 or 10 years younger than their family member was diagnosed, whichever comes sooner — for our kids, that means being screened at 35. With double to triple the risk, I want to be as proactive as I can for my children — now ages 15 and 11 — and that means altering their diet (and ours!) to limit foods that may increase risk. We've read through current research and determined which changes are worth making. We don't plan to restrict them completely from all foods associated with higher risk because we realize that's unrealistic (and we want them to enjoy eating), but we'll teach them to savor these foods in moderation. We're limiting how often we eat some foods First, processed meats will largely be eliminated from their diet. Our bacon-loving sons have only enjoyed this delicacy as a treat during vacations, and that plan will continue. They'll only indulge in other processed meats like hot dogs or ham when served at a barbecue or other social gathering. And cold cuts have been eliminated from our home, except for sliced turkey from our local market, which they prepare in-house without additives like sodium nitrites or nitrates. Secondly, our kids love a medium-rare steak, and we don't plan to take that from them. But we will limit red meat to once a week or less, filling our other dinner menus with healthier protein like salmon, chicken, or turkey. In our home, sugary drinks have never been a staple. We don't keep soda in the house, and that's not going to change. Aside from Gatorade during workouts or sporting events, we'll continue focusing on increasing water intake for hydration. Fast food and other ultra-processed foods have no place in our home. Will my children have McDonald's once or twice a year? Perhaps they will, because my husband is easily persuaded by their happiness! But luckily, I have the time and ability to prepare home-cooked dinners most nights, and I don't plan to stop. Finally, we've talked with our kids about the dangers of alcohol since they were little, but that conversation will now include the fact that alcohol intake is a risk factor for several types of cancer, colorectal cancer included. We're also increasing how much we eat other things We're limiting consumption of some things but increasing how often we eat others. There are certain foods that promote colon health , and we'll make sure they know which ones do. We'll aim for a diet including calcium-rich dairy products, whole grains, fish, and fruits and vegetables. While our kids may not be receptive to every healthy option now (we struggle with vegetable intake just like many parents!), my hope is that the more we offer these foods and talk about a healthy diet with them, the likelier they are to adopt these eating habits as they grow. Our kids aren't thrilled that some of the foods they love are being limited — and they likely won't follow every suggestion when they're older — but it's our job to guide them down a healthy path and provide them with the necessary information, especially given their increased risk. Thankfully, my husband's story had a happy ending, and we were given the chance to change the trajectory for our kids. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Protestors Ransack AI Lab, Leave Graffiti Calling on Masses to “Burn the Data Centers”
items.summary: With anxiety over an AI doomsday reaching a fever pitch, some citizens of the world are no longer asking for regulations. Earlier this week, the offices of two Canadian AI labs were ransacked by what police officers describe as an organized group of vandals. According to the CBC , an office building belonging to Quebec’s Artificial Intelligence Institute (MILA) in Montreal was defaced. Its windows were smashed out and its walls defaced with anti-AI graffiti. Another building nearby, belonging to an unnamed AI company, was also vandalized. Images shared by the CBC show one of the tags spray painted on the building, which reads “burn the data centers.” “According to preliminary findings from the investigation, it appears that a group of about 10 individuals committed the crimes,” Manual Couture, a spokesperson for the Montreal police said in a statement reported by CTV News . “The windows of the building were smashed and numerous graffiti tags were sprayed on the walls.” At least one 25-year-old woman found near the scene was hauled in for questioning, CBC reported, though was later released without conditions. The vandalism comes amidst growing backlash against AI and the data centers that empower its growth. Scores of people have been arrested in the United States after protesting or defying municipal leaders during local meetings. The temperature is rising to such a level that the social risk to AI data center development in the US alone threatened some $130 billion worth of investments as of mid-August. The vandalism in Montreal is just a microcosm of that popular anti-AI sentiment — showing that if people continue to be ignored by their elected officials, they’re not afraid to take matters into their own hands. More on AI backlash: Protesters Arrested After Storming OpenAI Lobbying Office The post Protestors Ransack AI Lab, Leave Graffiti Calling on Masses to “Burn the Data Centers” appeared first on Futurism .

items.title: The leader of PwC's 2,200-person DC office says clients expect some consulting work twice as fast as a year ago
items.summary: Jeanelle Johnson, managing partner of PwC in the Washington DC area PwC AI is raising clients' expectations for faster delivery times on consulting projects. Jeanelle Johnson, PwC's DC managing partner, said clients now expect some work to be delivered in half the time. Faster delivery should not be confused with less work, said Johnson. AI is resetting assumptions about how quickly professional services firms should move, and consulting clients are getting impatient. "I am seeing clients ask for our help in delivering outcomes at a more rapid pace" compared to this time last year, Jeanelle Johnson, PwC's managing partner for the Washington DC area, told Business Insider. "Something that we might have said takes eight to 10 weeks; the expectation is probably half of that. The shelf life is half," Johnson said. Clients are not necessarily expecting an entire transformation to be completed in a fraction of the time; the expectation is more for pilots and proofs of concepts, she said. "There's an expectation now that tools should accelerate the work," she added. Johnson leads more than 2,200 consulting and accounting employees in her role as PwC's DC managing partner. Asked whether those compressed timelines were putting pressure on her consulting teams, she said: "We're working on it." The Big Four professional services firms — PwC, Deloitte, KPMG, and EY — alongside firms like McKinsey, BCG, and Accenture, are at the center of the AI shift sweeping through workplaces. They have raced to build internal chatbots, train staff, and test AI in client work. The technology can now assist with, and increasingly perform, early-stage consulting tasks such as market research, due diligence, and brainstorming. At McKinsey, AI has accelerated the early problem-solving cycle, turning what used to be a team's "week one answer" — the first hypothesis after a week of research and analysis — into an "hour one answer," Kate Smaje, McKinsey's Global Leader for technology and AI, told Business Insider in June. That frees up consultants to spend more time testing deeper parts of the issue tree rather than waiting days to get oriented, Smaje said. Have a tip or story to share about working in consulting? Contact this reporter via email at pthompson@businessinsider.com or Signal at Polly_Thompson.89. Use a personal email address, a nonwork WiFi network, and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely . Amid the rank and file, employees at top firms have told Business Insider they're seeing a difference in delivery times due to AI. A software engineer at Deloitte US told Business Insider that some coding tasks had fallen from a dayslong process to around five minutes with AI, and an EY-Parthenon consultant in the UK said that due diligence that previously took two weeks of manual work and spreadsheet handling can now be completed in a day with AI. As well as pressure to deliver faster results, the shift is also raising questions about how the pricing model that has rested on human labor will adapt as more work gets done by AI. The work is more complex For Johnson, faster delivery should not be confused with less work. AI will change how consultants spend their time , freeing capacity for more meaningful or higher-value work rather than simply reducing the number of hours needed on a project, she told Business Insider. The work itself is also becoming more complex, she added. Clients are navigating geopolitical tensions, wars, tariffs, and macroeconomic uncertainty simultaneously — a broader set of pressures than consultants would often have helped them tackle in the past. "The confluence of all those things at the same time is something that we used to deal with one or two things at a time," Johnson said. "Now we're in a world order where we have to deal with 10 plus, plus, plus at a time." Read the original article on Business Insider

Have a tip or story to share about working in consulting? Contact this reporter via email at pthompson@businessinsider.com or Signal at Polly_Thompson.89. Use a personal email address, a nonwork WiFi network, and a nonwork device; here's our guide to sharing information securely.

Amid the rank and file, employees at top firms have told Business Insider they're seeing a difference in delivery times due to AI.

A software engineer at Deloitte US told Business Insider that some coding tasks had fallen from a dayslong process to around five minutes with AI, and an EY-Parthenon consultant in the UK said that due diligence that previously took two weeks of manual work and spreadsheet handling can now be completed in a day with AI.

As well as pressure to deliver faster results, the shift is also raising questions about how the pricing model that has rested on human labor will adapt as more work gets done by AI.

The work is more complex

For Johnson, faster delivery should not be confused with less work.

AI will change how consultants spend their time, freeing capacity for more meaningful or higher-value work rather than simply reducing the number of hours needed on a project, she told Business Insider.

The work itself is also becoming more complex, she added. Clients are navigating geopolitical tensions, wars, tariffs, and macroeconomic uncertainty simultaneously — a broader set of pressures than consultants would often have helped them tackle in the past.

"The confluence of all those things at the same time is something that we used to deal with one or two things at a time," Johnson said.

"Now we're in a world order where we have to deal with 10 plus, plus, plus at a time."

items.title: “Slop Grenades”: Shopify CEO Who Pushed Staff to Use AI Is Now Horrified by What He’s Wrought
items.summary: Shopify CEO Tobias Lütke is getting a first-hand look at the AI-workplace revolution, and it isn’t a pretty sight. New reporting by Fortune revealed the disastrous results of Shopify’s all-out scramble to embrace AI nearly a year ago. After telling workers that using AI tools is a “baseline expectation” in the workplace, Lütke is now changing his tune as workers spew out AI-generated emails, memos, and code without double-checking it beforehand. “We call those ‘slop grenades’ that people toss at each other,” Lütke said in an interview on the Knowledge Project podcast . “That’s definitely a bad thing.” The CEO further explained that the initiative incentivized workers to “go nuts” on AI, leading to a deluge of AI generated slop. “You don’t really read it, and now it has to be reviewed by your colleagues, and they are like, ‘this doesn’t look right,'” he complained. “You’re just letting AI do the work for you.” As ironic as it may be for the once-AI-happy Shopify exec, he’s far from alone. An April survey of 1,150 office workers found that 40 percent had encountered a phenomenon known as “workslop,” or AI-generated content that looks professional on the surface but lacks any actual substance. Estimates found workers already waste 3.4 hours a month cleaning up the AI schlock, amounting to a monthly loss of $8.1 million for a workplace with 10,000 employees. Another survey from earlier in September found that negative sentiments around AI in workplace have exploded over the past few years, with the majority of workers now expressing negative attitudes toward the tech. Whatever way you slice it, it’s clear that AI is not a catch-all for workplace productivity — an obnoxious lesson Shopify’s Lütke had to learn the hard way. More on AI: AI Really Is Eviscerating Entry-Level Jobs, New Data Shows The post “Slop Grenades”: Shopify CEO Who Pushed Staff to Use AI Is Now Horrified by What He’s Wrought appeared first on Futurism .

items.title: ‘Supermountains’ Buried Under Antarctica Fueled Explosion of Life, Scientists Discover
items.summary: Welcome back to the Abstract! These are the studies this week that ate well, moved mountains, grew brains, and saved medieval texts. First, scientists set out to understand why Venus doesn’t have a moon and discover even more unnerving stuff about this delightfully nightmarish planet. Then: a hidden range of primordial supermountains, a literal brain-space, and evidence of Tudor-era subterfuge. As always, for more of my work, check out my book First Contact: The Story of Our Obsession with Aliens , or subscribe to my personal newsletter the BeX Files . I’m so hungry I could eat my own moon Kane, Stephen R. et al. “Tidal Demise: The Evolution and Fate of a Hypothetical Venus Moon.” The Astrophysical Journal. Venus is a bizarro world with a year that is shorter than its day, a surface shaped by diabolical heat and pressure, and skies soaked in sulfuric acid. Frankly, this planet is metal enough as it is, but scientists have now suggested that Venus is also a moon-eater. For years, researchers have pondered why Venus lacks a moon, in contrast to all other planets except Mercury. One possibility is that Venus was once orbited by a primordial satellite that it ultimately tore apart and swallowed, according to a new study. And honestly, that sounds like something Venus would do. It’s in character. Venus as captured by Mariner 10 in the 1970s. Image: NASA To reach this conclusion, scientists ran simulations of Venusian moons ranging from half to ten times as massive as Earth’s Moon. Because Venus has a very slow rotation rate equal to 243 Earth days, most of the modeled satellites were drawn inward, ultimately crashing into Venus. Earth’s fast rotation rate, in contrast, has pushed the Moon to recede farther from our world, at a rate of about 1.5 inches each year. “The absence of a Venusian satellite can be understood as a natural consequence of tidal evolution alone,” said researchers led by Stephen Kane of the University of California, Riverside. The researchers added that the obliteration of a past moon around Venus may offer one reason why the planet became so aggressively inhospitable, while Earth evolved into a comfy haven for life. “The fate of a Venus moon carries direct implications for early Venus habitability,” the team said. “The eventual destruction of the moon…would deliver a massive energy pulse to the Venusian surface and atmosphere, with potential implications for the loss of surface water and the onset of a runaway greenhouse state.” It’s possible that NASA’s DAVINCI orbiter, which is due for launch to Venus in 2029, could search for the chemical signatures of an ancient obliterated moon, according to the study. In the meantime, my takeaway is that Majora’s Mask is based on a true Venusian story. In other news… If it’s not Gondwana, I don’t wanna Chen, Bei and Campbell, Ian H. “Do Himalayan-style mountains lie under the Antarctic ice: Implication for the Gondwana Supermountains, the rise of oxygen and the Cambrian explosion?” Earth and Planetary Science Letters. Shout out to my fellow Gondwana-heads! Just a week after a study came out minting Gondwana as a bonafide “supercontinent,” another work has probedthe remnants of Himalaya-scale “Gondwana supermountains” buried deep under Antarctica’s ice sheet. Both studies argue that the geological upheaval associated with Gondwana’s formation directly led to the Cambrian “explosion” of complex life that began about 538 million years ago. But the new study focuses on the role of Gondwana’s colossal mountain range and the massive submarine “fan” system underneath it. Reconstruction of Gondwana highlighting core blocks, interior orogens and peripheral orogens. Image: Chen, Bei and Campbell, Ian H. “It is unlikely to be a coincidence that Earth’s most dramatic period of evolution correlates with the planet’s most important period of mountain building: the formation and erosion of the Gondwana Supermountains,” said authors Bei Chen and Ian H. Campbell of the Australian National University. By studying 1,700 zircons—hardy minerals that can be used to reconstruct continental timelines—the researchers found a disproportionate spike in Antarctic zircons dating from 650 and 450 million years ago, consistent with the formation of Gondwana. The supermountains and their underlying fan systems provided the necessary nutrients for the meteoric rise of animals and other complex life in the Cambrian period, according to the study. “Analyses of detrital zircons from Antarctica show that its tectonics were dominated by Himalayan-style mountains, the roots of which now underlie the ice sheet,” the team concluded. Gondwana broke apart during the age of dinosaurs, but as these studies show, its body parts live on, scattered under ice and dispersed across new continents. This has been Gondwana News. Occupy Mouse Brain Konstantin Kaganovsky, Kevin W. Kelley, Tilo Gschwind, Paul M. Harary et al. “Developmental xenocortication using human-derived organoids in mice.” Nature. It is notoriously challenging to study human brain tissue in vivo on both practical and ethical levels. It’s not as if you can just cut open someone’s noggin and rummage around in there like you’re Victor Frankenstein. But scientists have now discovered a promising workaround by transplanting human brain “organoids”—lab-grown structures based on human stem cells—into the heads of mice that have been engineered to have open space in their brains instead of a cortex. Scientists who developed this new experimental technique of “xenocortication” report that the human organoids grew to occupy the cavities in the rodents’ heads, and showed analogous development to real brain tissues. The xenocortical (abbreviated XCX, no relation to Charli) mice seemed to behave more or less normally, despite having millions of human-derived neurons in their heads. Graphic showing the human organoid transplanted into the mouse brain. Image: Konstantin Kaganovsky, Kevin W. Kelley, Tilo Gschwind, Paul M. Harary et al. “We envision that xenocortication will be useful for obtaining circuit- and behaviour-level readouts using human neurons to study neurodevelopment, model disease and develop therapeutics,” said researchers co-led by Konstantin Kaganovsky, Kevin W. Kelley, Tilo Gschwind, and Paul M. Harary of Stanford University. “Generating XCX mice with more mature and canonical cortical organization will require early and proactive engagement to establish ethical guidance,” the team emphasized. Talk about living rent-free in someone else’s head. Hard to Gage his motivation Walter, Katie and Wade, James. “Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ: A missing fragment from Takamiya MS 20 in the holdings of The Keep.” Notes and Queries. King Henry VIII, the English monarch notorious for disposing of wives and Catholic hegemony, relied on the courtier Sir John Gage to dissolve and plunder monasteries during his consequential reign. But the discovery of long-lost pages that were once possessed by Gage reveals that this royal ally may have saved an outlawed manuscript from destruction, hinting at a dangerous act of subterfuge. Pages 8-9 of The Keep fragment of Nicholas Love’s early 15th-century Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ with visible thread binding. Image: Courtesy of The Trustees of the Firle Estate Settlement and the University of Sussex Katie Walter of the University of Sussex and James Wade of Girton College, Cambridge identified a six-page fragment of a popular medieval text that had been misplaced within Gage’s belongings. The fragment came from Nicholas Love’s Mirror of the Blessed Life of Jesus Christ, which was popular in the 15th century, but had fallen out of favor by Henry VIII’s reign. It seems that Gage nonetheless saved a copy, despite orders to destroy such texts. “One consequence of this puzzle is that the fragment, hereafter referred to as The Keep fragment, has gone undescribed,” said Walter and Wade in their new study. “John Gage possibly acquired the book at the time of the dissolution of the monasteries” and it later became “hidden in plain sight” in his belongings. And Gage would have gotten away with it too, if it weren’t for those meddling historians! Thanks for reading! See you next week.

items.title: Rings around a tiny body have changed over the past decade
items.summary: For decades, astronomers thought rings were something only giant planets had. That changed in 2013, when a small, dark body orbiting between Saturn and Uranus passed in front of a star and blinked twice on either side of the main event, revealing two narrow rings around an object barely 250 kilometers across. “It was a surprise,” says Pablo Santos-Sanz, an astronomer at the Instituto de Astrofísica de Andalucía in Granada, Spain. Ever since, the question has been what such rings are made of and how long they can last. In a recent study, Santos-Sanz and his colleagues used the James Webb Space Telescope to watch the same body, now known as Chariklo, pass in front of a background star again. They found one of its rings had grown denser and the other had almost vanished. We don’t know exactly why. Shadowing a star The technique behind the observation is simple. “We predict when a Solar System object passes in front of a star,” Santos-Sanz said. The starlight dims for a moment, and the shape of that dip reveals the size, shape, and surroundings of the object that caused it. “This is particularly challenging for minor bodies, and more challenging for distant minor bodies,” he said. Read full article Comments

items.title: Inside the squishy nightmare: Explosions, burns, and thousands of calls to poison control
items.summary: Jim Franco/Albany Times Union via Getty Images; Rebecca Zisser/BI Warning: Some of the images you may see are graphic. For questions or if you suspect a poisoning, contact Poison Help at PoisonHelp.org or call 1-800-222-1222. Katie Zerbst was doing laundry on a Sunday morning in June when she heard a "guttural" moan. "It was the sound that makes you just drop everything and run," the 45-year-old mother told Business Insider. Rushing into the kitchen, Zerbst found her 10-year-old daughter, Violet, covered in steaming hot, sparkly goo. Burns seared across her face, and skin from her top lip was flapping down into her mouth. Moments earlier, Violet had popped a squishy toy into the microwave for 30 seconds. She wanted to make the glittery cube more malleable so she could squish it more easily. When she pulled it out, it erupted like a volcano. Violet ended up in the emergency room, and she isn't the only child to visit the hospital after playing with a squishy. Violet Zerbst, 10, suffered burns on her face and body after a squishy toy exploded. Katie Zerbst Business Insider reviewed dozens of incident reports, spoke to parents, and consulted doctors and regulators about the risks behind this year's biggest toy craze. Despite a spike in reports of burns and concerns about toxic exposure, oversight of squishies — slime-filled toys shaped like dumplings, fruit, ice cubes, and other cute characters — falls into a regulatory gray area, and the market is teeming with counterfeits and knockoffs. Have a squishy story to share? Reach out to Business Insider correspondent Jane Ridley: jridley@businessinsider.com. What's in a squishy? Squishies, with their gooey, foamy, or gel-like textures, fall into the category of "sensory toys," like fidget spinners, kinetic sand, and magnetic balls. In recent years, the toys have gone "from zero to hero," Five Below CEO Winnie Park told investors in June. They're helping the retailer to become "America's greatest little toy store" by driving brick-and-mortar traffic, Park said on September's earnings call. Kohl's also credited the toy with a sales bump, and workers from several retailers have taken to social media with tales of over-eager customers demanding their favorite squishies. Instagram and TikTok are full of satisfying videos of hands squishing toys shaped like a strawberry or a tube of toothpaste. However, reports from homes and hospitals across the country describe exploding and leaking toys, along with chemical smells. America's Poison Centers told Business Insider that more than half of the 11,500 reports about squishies received by its member organizations since 2024 happened in the first six months of 2026, though only a small portion of the ruptures caused severe injury. Schylling, which manufactures the most popular squishy brand, NeeDoh, was hit with two lawsuits in July over squishy explosions that plaintiffs say resulted in severe burns. One complaint said that a NeeDoh Nice Cube, left lying on a TV stand near a window, remained cool to the touch but, when squeezed, erupted with a scalding gel that left blisters on the person's leg. Lawyers for the company declined to comment on the allegations. The US Consumer Product Safety Commission has also seen a spike in squishy-related incident reports from shoppers and hospitals this year. A Business Insider review found about two dozen consumers describing how ruptures — due to microwaves, hot cars, and squeezing — have burned kids this year. Roughly 20 more reported strong smells emanating from the squishy toys . Hospital reports collected by CPSC showed about a dozen explosion cases in 2025, the latest year available. One parent told the CPSC the toy didn't "just pop"; it "exploded" in February 2024 after their daughter squeezed it on her 10th birthday. This August, another reported that their 8-year-old son was squeezing his squishy normally when it ruptured. "The outer layer of the toy failed without warning, spraying the internal filling directly across my son's face and into his eyes," causing immediate "burning and distress," the report said. A February report to CPSC echoed a common complaint about a squishy that "emitted an extremely powerful and persistent chemical odor, resembling acetone or nail polish remover," which gave its owner a headache. In response to growing public concern, the CPSC issued guidance in August, warning shoppers of serious burn hazards from intentionally or unintentionally exposing toys to heat. A spokesperson told Business Insider that these toys hit on several longstanding concerns for the agency, including the dangers of water beads and potential exposure to unsafe chemicals. As for the dangers of microwaving them? That's considered improper use, and the agency doesn't typically punish companies when consumers don't follow safety warnings, the spokesperson said. Underlying these reports is the common frustration that squishy ingredients vary widely and often aren't listed on the packaging. NeeDoh discloses that its products, including the Nice Cube, Dream Drop, and Groovy Glob, use fairly common ingredients such as maltose sugar, cornstarch, and polyvinyl alcohol, the latter of which the brand says is non-toxic and also found in white glue. While these ingredients are considered chemically safe, the lawsuit in California cites academic research to argue that some of these substances have thermal properties that, along with a soft polymer casing, can make scalding hot gel feel deceptively cool to the touch — until the toy pops. The market is also rife with knock-offs, and federal safety rules are patchy. US regulations don't require independent testing and certification of toys, unless they're marketed to children under 13. Manufacturers initially decide how to market and age-grade their products, subject to CPSC oversight. While products clearly intended for young children, such as baby pacifiers or toddler teethers, must meet stricter testing requirements, squishies can plausibly be sold as children's toys, adult stress balls, desk accessories, or collectibles. Many are marketed as products for all ages, and verifying a toy's age classification can involve a lengthy review. That ambiguity raises a broader question: When an all-ages product becomes wildly popular with children, should it be treated as a children's toy ? Violet ended up in the emergency room, and she isn't the only child to visit the hospital after playing with a squishy.

Violet Zerbst, 10, suffered burns on her face and body after a squishy toy exploded.

Despite a spike in reports of burns and concerns about toxic exposure, oversight of squishies — slime-filled toys shaped like dumplings, fruit, ice cubes, and other cute characters — falls into a regulatory gray area, and the market is teeming with counterfeits and knockoffs.

Squishies, with their gooey, foamy, or gel-like textures, fall into the category of "sensory toys," like fidget spinners, kinetic sand, and magnetic balls.

items.title: This week’s news from Zed, Anthropic, and OpenRouter shows why better harnesses matter more than better models
items.summary: Our five most-read stories this week covered code collaboration, a model router, a UI change, a benchmark, and a caching tutorial. Five different stories about the same problem: Turning a model into something users can actually use. That’s the harness: The software around the model that supplies context, connects tools, routes work, and checks results. Zed was the big news this week and is rebuilding how people review agent-written code. OpenRouter is giving companies more control over where requests are processed. Anthropic is rebuilding its stack to be less confusing. The benchmark shows where coding agents still struggle, and the tutorial explains when you can skip a model call entirely. Late in the week, Vercel’s AI Gateway reported that the average price per token fell 23.2% in August, the third straight monthly decline. Inference is getting cheaper. Companies are buying the harness around inference now, and Zed, OpenRouter, and Anthropic all spent this week selling it. Zed and Anthropic are removing blockers On Wednesday, two companies took aim at a familiar problem: getting people to organize work before they can do it. Zed launched Delta in public beta, building code collaboration around shared threads instead of pull requests. Anthropic began rolling Claude Chat and Cowork into one interface , removing the upfront decisions about which mode a task belongs in. Paul Sawers reported the Zed story for The New Stack . It was our runaway piece of the week, drawing more than double the traffic of anything else. Zed is clearly onto something. Zed CEO Nathan Sobo said it best: “It seems like everyone is in a race to replace GitHub right now.” His argument is that a diff shows you where an agent landed, but leaves much of the conversation that got it there somewhere else. Delta keeps that conversation attached to the code, while DeltaDB records changes at edit-level granularity. Zed says 33 of its team members landed 570 changes to Delta’s main branch without opening a single pull request. That’s Delta’s own repository; the public Zed editor repository still accepts conventional pull requests. Meanwhile, GitHub reported 2.9 billion monthly commits in August, up from 1.4 billion in April. This was despite GitHub crashing for nearly eight hours in August. Sobo thinks the thread will become software development’s fundamental unit. And Zed is not on this quest to replace GitHub alone. Cursor’s Origin and GitLab’s Project Switch are other takes on rebuilding code collaboration for agents. Anthropic is tackling a different user handoff. This week, it announced a unified interface bringing Cowork’s capabilities into Claude Chat. The goal is to reduce confusion and merge capabilities. The rollout starts with Pro and Max users, with other plans following. “People used both, and told us the frustrating part was deciding where a task belonged,” the company said, as Amanda Caswell reported. I’ve been using it since the switch, and removing the choice was the right call. Now, users should more easily grasp the capabilities and workflow possible with Cowork. The economics make the harness matter even more OpenRouter’s US in-region routing is now generally available to business and enterprise customers. Requests sent through its US endpoint are decrypted, processed, and served inside the country, or rejected if that guarantee can’t be met. Sawers wrote that story too. One number explains the demand: Open-weight models accounted for roughly 60% of OpenRouter’s US-originating token consumption in August, with Chinese models making up most of the volume. DeepSeek V4 Pro, Kimi K3, GLM 5.2. These are models developed in China and available through providers running them in US data centers The models’ country of origin and the location where your data gets processed are different questions. OpenRouter is selling control over the second one. That matters, since Deloitte’s global survey cited in the story found that 77% of companies factor an AI solution’s country of origin into vendor selection. Stripe’s announced acquisition of OpenRouter, reportedly worth about $8 billion, adds another measure of the interest in this layer. Vercel’s September AI Gateway Production Index , published September 17, shows the economics from another angle: Open weights took the volume. Closed models kept the money. Share of tokens against share of spending on Vercel’s AI Gateway, August 2026. Models Share of tokens Share of estimated spend Open-weight models 56% 14% Closed-weight models 44% 86% Anthropic, all models n/a 64% GPT-6 Astra, first 12 days after Sept. 3 launch n/a 7.7% Source: Vercel AI Gateway Production Index , Sept. 17, 2026. Gateway traffic only; spending is estimated from labs’ published list prices, so actual bills may differ. Open weight crossed into the majority of Vercel’s gateway token volume for the first time, up from a reported 7% in December 2025. Vercel says its current open-weight classification is broader than the one used in earlier reports. Among teams running more than ten million tokens in both comparison months, the median team paid 7.6% less per token, following July’s 2.9% decline. So what justifies the premium? Boris Renski, CEO of AI agent integration company Apelogic, argues that much of it buys enterprise plumbing: identity integration, connectors, and observability. In Adrian Bridgwater’s July reporting , CNCF executive director Jonathan Bryce described paying ten times more for a four-month capability lead as “a very expensive form of lock-in.” Closed models still command most of the estimated spending, and customers may be paying for capabilities that cheaper alternatives don’t reliably deliver. But cheaper inference raises the pressure on everything around it, and Anthropic spent its week on exactly that. Instead of making headlines with a new model, it shipped a merged interface, documents and slides — features arguably more important to most users. The harness has to earn its keep Amanda Caswell covered Real-SWE , a benchmark from Y Combinator-backed Specific Labs built on private codebases from real companies. The best setup tested, Claude Fable 5.1 running through Claude Code, succeeded 38.8% of the time. GPT-6 Astra through Codex CLI reached 33.8%; Gemini 3.8 Flash through Gemini CLI reached 31.2%. None broke 40%. The benchmark is small: 10 tasks, with eight attempts per model on each. And it tests models with their coding tools, so the harness is already in the score. Still, no model solved the analytics stream reducer across 64 attempts. Zero. Solutions touched a median of 11 files, compared with six in the public benchmarks cited in the reporting. Real work is spread out. These agents struggled to follow it. Fable’s leading failure categories were missed requirements and integration errors. That doesn’t mean the information was missing. An agent can have it and still overlook it, misunderstand it, or skip the check. The engineering problem is getting context, tools, and verification to work together. So is knowing when the model doesn’t need to run at all. Abhilash Rao Mesala, a senior data engineer at Meta, wrote a practical guide to LLM response caching for us: reuse an answer when the request, context, permissions, and underlying information make it valid. His example starts with a million calls a month at $0.006 each, or $6,000. A 60% cache hit rate, plus $150 in embedding and vector-store costs, brings that to $2,550. A 57.5% reduction from a principle older than the transformer. The hard part is knowing when a stored answer is still the right answer. Pair Mesala’s piece with Ida Silfverskiöld’s on Towards Data Science guide to saving on tokens , which covers prompt caching, model routing, and keeping unnecessary materials out of an agent’s context. Both are worth your time. It’s hard to ignore the doom and gloom hovering over AI at the moment. But there’s good news out there, too. Each week, the price of inference is dropping, and companies are improving harnesses – both are critical improvements to push AI into the mainstream. The post This week’s news from Zed, Anthropic, and OpenRouter shows why better harnesses matter more than better models appeared first on The New Stack .

Source: Vercel AI Gateway Production Index, Sept. 17, 2026. Gateway traffic only; spending is estimated from labs’ published list prices, so actual bills may differ.

Open weight crossed into the majority of Vercel’s gateway token volume for the first time, up from a reported 7% in December 2025. Vercel says its current open-weight classification is broader than the one used in earlier reports. Among teams running more than ten million tokens in both comparison months, the median team paid 7.6% less per token, following July’s 2.9% decline.

So what justifies the premium? 

Boris Renski, CEO of AI agent integration company Apelogic, argues that much of it buys enterprise plumbing: identity integration, connectors, and observability. In Adrian Bridgwater’s July reporting, CNCF executive director Jonathan Bryce described paying ten times more for a four-month capability lead as “a very expensive form of lock-in.”

Closed models still command most of the estimated spending, and customers may be paying for capabilities that cheaper alternatives don’t reliably deliver.

But cheaper inference raises the pressure on everything around it, and Anthropic spent its week on exactly that. Instead of making headlines with a new model, it shipped a merged interface, documents and slides — features arguably more important to most users.

The harness has to earn its keep

Amanda Caswell covered Real-SWE, a benchmark from Y Combinator-backed Specific Labs built on private codebases from real companies. 

The best setup tested, Claude Fable 5.1 running through Claude Code, succeeded 38.8% of the time. GPT-6 Astra through Codex CLI reached 33.8%; Gemini 3.8 Flash through Gemini CLI reached 31.2%. None broke 40%. 

The benchmark is small: 10 tasks, with eight attempts per model on each. And it tests models with their coding tools, so the harness is already in the score. Still, no model solved the analytics stream reducer across 64 attempts. Zero.

Solutions touched a median of 11 files, compared with six in the public benchmarks cited in the reporting. Real work is spread out. These agents struggled to follow it. 

Fable’s leading failure categories were missed requirements and integration errors. That doesn’t mean the information was missing. An agent can have it and still overlook it, misunderstand it, or skip the check.

The engineering problem is getting context, tools, and verification to work together. So is knowing when the model doesn’t need to run at all. 

Abhilash Rao Mesala, a senior data engineer at Meta, wrote a practical guide to LLM response caching for us: reuse an answer when the request, context, permissions, and underlying information make it valid. His example starts with a million calls a month at $0.006 each, or $6,000. A 60% cache hit rate, plus $150 in embedding and vector-store costs, brings that to $2,550. A 57.5% reduction from a principle older than the transformer.

The hard part is knowing when a stored answer is still the right answer.

Pair Mesala’s piece with Ida Silfverskiöld’s on Towards Data Science guide to saving on tokens, which covers prompt caching, model routing, and keeping unnecessary materials out of an agent’s context. Both are worth your time. 

It’s hard to ignore the doom and gloom hovering over AI at the moment. But there’s good news out there, too. Each week, the price of inference is dropping, and companies are improving harnesses – both are critical improvements to push AI into the mainstream.

items.title: Warren Buffett has stepped down as Berkshire chairman. Here are 5 leadership lessons he leaves behind.
items.summary: Warren Buffett's decades leading Berkshire Hathaway yielded numerous lessons, including learning from mistakes. Nati Harnik/AP This week, the Oracle of Omaha gave up his job of chairman of Berkshire Hathaway. After decades at the top, Warren Buffett leaves a legacy of leadership advice. He has emphasized the importance of self-improvement, honesty, and choosing the right leaders. If you want to be a high-mileage leader like Warren Buffett, it pays to be humble. The Oracle of Omaha this week gave up the job as chairman of Berkshire Hathaway, after more than half a century spent building and then running the conglomerate. Buffett said his son Howard would succeed him as chairman. In that role, his son will guard Berkshire's culture and values, which the elder Buffett said are "worth more than anything on our balance sheet." That belief in the importance of organizational culture is nothing new for Buffett who has, over the years, offered a steady stream of advice on investing and leadership. Last year, in his final Thanksgiving letter to shareholders as CEO, he shared insights on the virtues of stewardship, honesty, and what he described as "good intentions" gone awry in attempts to rein in CEO pay. One broad takeaway was his call to continue learning and growing. "Choose your heroes very carefully and then emulate them. You will never be perfect, but you can always be better," Buffett wrote. Here are five other lessons Buffett shared: Stay humble The 96-year-old famously ran Berkshire with an unfussy, meat-and-potatoes sensibility. Buffett wrote about the role luck played in his life and work, and how that experience continually honed his sense of humility. "Keep in mind that the cleaning lady is as much a human being as the Chairman," Buffett said. He also grounded some of his humble inclinations in the luck he had, being a man — compared with his sisters, whom he described as having "equal intelligence and better personalities," though they faced a much different outlook. "I was born in 1930 healthy, reasonably intelligent, white, male and in America. Wow! Thank you, Lady Luck," he said. Learn from your errors Buffett said that while he's made many mistakes, he's tried to use them as springboards for growth. "Learn at least a little from them and move on," Buffett wrote. One misstep, he said, was not intervening more forcefully when he saw indications that a "wonderful and loyal CEO" of a parent or subsidiary company would "succumb to dementia, Alzheimer's or another debilitating and long-term disease." "Charlie and I encountered this problem several times and failed to act. This failure can be a huge mistake," Buffett wrote, referring to Charlie Munger, his longtime friend and colleague, who died in 2023. Buffett said that while it's often not easy, boards need to keep watch for signs of such conditions in chiefs, and that CEOs themselves need to do the same at the units they oversee. "Directors should be alert and speak up is all that I can advise," Buffett said in the letter, which ran about seven pages. Choose the right leaders Part of Buffett's call for humility extended to how future Berkshire leaders should expect to conduct themselves — and what they should aspire to. He said that the company should only require five or six CEOs over the next century. In the shareholder letter released Friday, Buffett reiterated his confidence in Greg Abel, who succeeded him as CEO. "He has been making the decisions that matter for some time now, and I have not had to think twice about any of them," Buffett wrote. Buffett wrote last fall that he wanted Berkshire Hathaway, which was a New England textile producer when he began buying up its stock in the early 1960s, to avoid hiring top leaders who are there for the wrong reasons: "It should particularly avoid those whose goal is to retire at 65, to become look-at-me rich or to initiate a dynasty," Buffett said of the company. Think about your obit One recurring theme in his letter centered on Buffett's assertion that it's "never too late to improve." Another bit of advice: Work backward from what you want your obituary to say and then "live the life to deserve it." The release of Buffett's third annual Thanksgiving letter to Berkshire shareholders had become something of an event because of his status as one of the world's most famous investors. He said at the time that he planned to continue to address shareholders in an annual letter , though not as CEO. "As the British would say, I'm 'going quiet.' Sort of." Don't rule from the grave Buffett's decision to become chairman emeritus appeared in line with his advice against of trying to retain influence for too long. In his Thanksgiving letter, Buffett applauded the abilities of Abel , who is some three decades younger and took over as CEO at the start of 2026. "He is a great manager, a tireless worker and an honest communicator," Buffett said. He also wrote about his three children, whom he said possess the "maturity, brains, energy and instincts" to disburse the family's large fortune . Earlier this year, Buffett's net worth was nearing $150 billion. After he dies, Buffett wrote last year, his children will be free to adapt to changes in tax policy and other factors as needed to continue the family's philanthropic work. "Ruling from the grave does not have a great record, and I have never had an urge to do so," he said. An earlier version of this story appeared on November 10, 2025. items.title: Microsoft’s AI CEO says ‘controlling’ AI ‘is going to be a really, really big challenge’
items.summary: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman Bloomberg/Getty Images Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman said AI labs need to ensure they can control what they're creating. "We should not create something that we can't control," Suleyman said. Suleyman questioned why some in tech are so opposed to new regulations. Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman says it's "surreal" that he has to say AI needs to align with humanity. "We should not create something that we can't control," Suleyman said Friday on CNBC's "Squawk Box." "And if it looks like we're on a path to producing something that is not just more powerful than all of us combined, but is, as a result, something that we can't control, then it's going to fail in its fundamental purpose." Success will not come easily, Suleyman said. "Controlling these things are going to be a really, really big challenge for us," he said. Suleyman said he was "glad to see a lot more people" supporting the idea that tech companies and frontier model makers need to maintain control over their AI systems. In the industry, ensuring AI acts in accordance with human intentions is called alignment. "But there's a growing group of people that think that we are doing it for its own sake, and we just want to turn over the next card, see what's around the corner, and create something that is just going to slip our own leash," he said. Suleyman's comments come at a time of increased attention to AI safety, after former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned that AI workers are privately fearful that AI could wipe out humanity. In recent days, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei , OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk have all expressed broad agreement that frontier AI labs should better pace their advancements to ensure that safety measures can keep up. Before Coxon's viral post, many in the industry were already concerned about safety after OpenAI revealed that its agents had breached Hugging Face , illustrating the potential consequences of losing control over AI systems. Suleyman called the breadth of the Hugging Face breach and OpenAI's initial unawareness of what its AI agents were doing "remarkable." "It has moved everybody from Elon and Zuck to me, Sam, Dario, and everybody else in between to say it's time that we take a look at this," Suleyman said. "I don't think it's overly alarmist. I don't think it's self-interested. I actually think it's responsible." Meta CEO Zuckerberg has taken a different stance than Amodei and other AI leaders. Earlier this week, Zuckerberg questioned why AI companies need to band together to manage the rate of development, suggesting that each company should handle its own business. "Every lab has the responsibility and incentive to move at the pace required to train its models safely," Zuckerberg wrote on X. Some in tech, including Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang , have questioned whether broad new regulations are needed. President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance have also pushed back on AI companies that are urging governments to act. Amodei and others have requested Congress and international bodies to get involved as well. Suleyman questioned those who scoff at the very idea of regulation. "Regulation is not a nasty, dangerous word," he said. "Everything that you trust and is of value at the moment has been carefully thought through by standards bodies that involve the industry, the public, consumer protection, Congress. And we're just going through that process." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Older Americans are sliding into poverty
items.summary: The supplemental poverty rate for older Americans has increased. Willowpix/Getty Images After a surge of pandemic-era aid, older Americans have faced rising poverty. Healthcare costs drive older Americans into poverty, straining their savings and finances. Social Security often isn't enough to cover costs, leading older Americans to take on low-paying jobs. After a slew of pandemic-induced aid ran its course, older Americans are falling back into poverty — and even younger would-be retirees are struggling. After the Great Recession, the trendline for older Americans had been improving, and 2020 pandemic relief measures helped buttress the aging population from falling into poverty in the wake of Covid. New census data shows that now, the poverty rate has increased the most for Americans 65 and older, after adjusting for things like tax credits and government programs. The share of all Americans living below that adjusted poverty measure grew from 9.1% in 2020 to 13.1% in 2025. For Americans 65 and older, that rate grew from 9.4% to 15.4%. Millions of older Americans live solely off Social Security benefits , which often don't cover all daily costs , let alone Medicare premiums or caregiving expenses. Social Security kept 28.8 million Americans out of poverty in 2025, the new Census report found, including nearly 21 million Americans 65 and older. As the boomer generation ages into retirement, those benefits look shaky, a worrying sign as lifespans stretch longer. Historically, poverty among older Americans rises with age, although younger retirement-aged Americans started falling into harder times as of 2024. Last year, Business Insider spoke with dozens of Americans 80 and older who were below or slightly above the poverty line, most of whom worked at least part time to make ends meet. Many said the only jobs they could find were minimum wage, menial jobs, paying them enough to put food on the table and heat their homes. Some said they had much more saved earlier in life, but were hit hard by medical treatments. "We should get tax breaks after a certain age because prices are so high for food," said Rebecca Reed, 88, who works two lower-paying jobs in New Orleans. "And maybe some discounts at the grocery store." Rebecca Reed works two part-time jobs at 88. Annie Flanagan for BI While the oldest Americans are still the most impoverished group, their younger counterparts have been seeing poverty rates tick up. The official poverty rate for Americans ages 70 to 74 saw the largest percentage-point increase from 2020 to 2024, according to a Business Insider analysis of Census microdata, followed by the younger cohort of 65- to 69-year-olds, indicating a more widely felt poverty landscape. Older Americans are often more prone to sudden and costly medical disruptions , which contribute to malnutrition or poor living conditions. Indeed, 7.7 million Americans fell into poverty due to medical expenses, per the Census report, and around 2.5 million of them were 65 and older. That's up from around 2.36 million in 2024. In interviews, dozens of families said they have spent six figures on care for their loved ones, as the median cost of a private nursing home room rose from $111,000 to $130,000 annually between 2022 and 2025, according to data from the care navigation platform CareScout. Some families said their older loved ones had exhausted all of their savings on home health aides or assisted living facilities, leaving them in the hands of their financially pressed children. Housing costs have also hurt many older Americans who don't own homes, or who have substantial home repairs. More than one in three older American households puts 30% or more of their income toward housing, per a 2025 study from Harvard University's Joint Center for Housing Studies . Older Americans are also the fastest-growing demographic experiencing homelessness, with about 20% of all people experiencing homelessness 55 and older as of 2024. Some are doing what they can to make the most of it. Sharon Albrecht, 85, works for a home healthcare agency and as a part-time Uber driver in Virginia to make ends meet. Though above the poverty line, Albrecht said her income goes a long way toward supplementing Social Security and her retirement savings, adding that she's "very wealthy in time and freedom to create my own schedule." "If an 80+ person has the attitude that 'Now, I have time to create,' the sky is the limit," Albrecht said. "It totally depends on the person and whether or not they have a victim mentality." items.title: I've spoken to my daughter in a non-native language since she was a baby. Now she corrects my French.
items.summary: The author has been speaking French to her daughter since she was a baby, even though it is not her native language. Courtesy of Tara McAllister. I hoped a bilingual upbringing would give my daughter an edge in life. I didn't realize that a non-native language to me would end up becoming our primary language. I've had my share of criticism over this decision, but it's working well for us so far. My daughter was born three months before the COVID-19 restrictions began where we live. Stuck at home with a new baby, I needed something to keep me busy, and I'm too mishap-prone for sourdough. For a linguist like me, a language-related project seemed like just the thing. I decided to dust off my French — which I spoke quite well in high school but hadn't used in decades — so I could speak it at home with my daughter. What parent hasn't heard about the benefits of bilingualism for little brains? Six years later, my project has outstripped all my expectations. We're lucky to have bilingual schools in our neighborhood. Because my daughter hears French from her peers as well as from me, she speaks it just as fluently as the English she uses with my husband and the rest of our family. My own ability to express myself in French grew little by little alongside hers. Today, we rarely speak English when it's just the two of us. Some people think I'm making a mistake My French is far from perfect: I'm never going to get rid of my American accent , and my speech is peppered with small mistakes — like le vidéo when it should be la vidéo . Sharing my family's language journey online, I've gotten criticism that my grammatical slips could harm my daughter's linguistic development. "If I wasn't fluent enough to not make errors, I would not be speaking that language to my child 100% of the time," one poster told me. Others have raised concerns about my emotional connection with my child. items.summary_html:
The author has been speaking French to her daughter since she was a baby, even though it is not her native language.

Courtesy of Tara McAllister.

  • I hoped a bilingual upbringing would give my daughter an edge in life.
  • I didn't realize that a non-native language to me would end up becoming our primary language.
  • I've had my share of criticism over this decision, but it's working well for us so far.

My daughter was born three months before the COVID-19 restrictions began where we live. Stuck at home with a new baby, I needed something to keep me busy, and I'm too mishap-prone for sourdough. For a linguist like me, a language-related project seemed like just the thing.

I decided to dust off my French — which I spoke quite well in high school but hadn't used in decades — so I could speak it at home with my daughter. What parent hasn't heard about the benefits of bilingualism for little brains?

Six years later, my project has outstripped all my expectations. We're lucky to have bilingual schools in our neighborhood. Because my daughter hears French from her peers as well as from me, she speaks it just as fluently as the English she uses with my husband and the rest of our family.

My own ability to express myself in French grew little by little alongside hers. Today, we rarely speak English when it's just the two of us.

Some people think I'm making a mistake

My French is far from perfect: I'm never going to get rid of my American accent, and my speech is peppered with small mistakes — like le vidéo when it should be la vidéo.

Sharing my family's language journey online, I've gotten criticism that my grammatical slips could harm my daughter's linguistic development. "If I wasn't fluent enough to not make errors, I would not be speaking that language to my child 100% of the time," one poster told me.

Others have raised concerns about my emotional connection with my child. "The optimal language of interaction is the caregiver's heart language (most dominant language)," a commenter on a bilingual-parenting blog warned.

The author said her daughter, now 6, often corrects her pronunciation.

Courtesy of Tara McAllister.

What the research shows

Since I'm a linguist by profession, I did a deep dive into the literature on bilingual development at the start of my project, and what I learned reinforced my decision to focus on French.

Many people believe that children are little sponges for language, but that's only half true. Children automatically soak up the language they hear in the surrounding community, especially from peers. But a language children hear mostly at home needs more encouragement to take root.

And even if they don't absorb the whole language overnight, children do have an advantage in certain aspects of language learning. My daughter doesn't imitate my accent and my grammatical errors. Instead, she corrects them. "Le vidéo doesn't make any sense, maman," she once told me in French.

The shared learning experience is invaluable

I once asked my husband if he thought speaking French was damaging my emotional connection with our daughter, who is now 6 years old. He snorted. "If anything, you have the opposite problem. You two are weirdly close," he told me.

It's true we have a very strong bond, what the French call une relation fusionnelle. And I suspect that our shared language journey has fostered that close connection rather than harming it.

Learning French is a project my daughter and I have shared for six years. Our current dynamic is unique: I still have a larger vocabulary and can teach her new words, but she is the one teaching me when it comes to pronunciation and certain aspects of grammar.

I do sometimes worry about the years to come. Will my French be strong enough to navigate the complexities of adolescence, for example. But it reassures me to watch my daughter slip effortlessly between English with her father and French with me. If her feelings become too complex to express in French, we can always pivot to the native language we share.

This summer, our family moved to France for a one-year sabbatical, so we will be discovering a new culture in addition to our language learning. Whatever languages we use in the future, this opportunity to broaden our horizons together will always remain precious.

items.title: Meta's Muse AI agent is very powerful — but not enough to overcome my kids' annoying school apps
items.summary: The Meta Muse AI agent, which acts as a personal assistant of sorts. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images I spent a week trying out Muse and gave it access to my email, credit cards, and even Apple health data. It was able to do some helpful tasks for me, like organizing my inbox, but failed at helping with school forms. Even though it failed fairly often, I imagine it will get better and more useful. I'm a convert! There are a whole slew of very good reasons that I should feel nervous about giving Meta access to my health data. Or my credit cards. Or read/write access to my personal and work emails and calendar. I think we can all reasonably agree that over the last 20 years, Meta has given reasonable people some very reasonable reasons to think that granting it that much access to personal, private data is very unreasonable. But I am not a reasonable person. Which is why I stopped worrying about AI killing us all and learned to love Muse , Meta's new AI agent. Well, mostly. Muse launched earlier this month and has received a surprisingly warm reaction. I guess I say surprising because Meta has struggled to launch an AI app that has caught on with consumers. Remember "Vibes," the video generating Sora competitor? Me neither. Muse's strength is that it's an easy-to-use and understand AI agent. You use it to send it to-do tasks like "organize my inbox" or "Find me a good travel stroller for my upcoming trip" instead of the more common things you use LLMs like ChatGPT for (such as text generation or in place of Google searching). Muse researches and offers to buy a travel stroller in this example from Meta's press release. Meta I started by testing it with some obvious, straightforward tasks. First, I asked it to look through my email and send me a daily digest of "important" emails (my inbox gets quickly clogged with PR pitches and newsletters). It did this admirably well. I also asked it to look at my credit and debit cards and tell me what subscription I could cancel — it suggested Flickr (for irrational reasons only understandable to my human soul, I'm keeping it). What more could I do? If I gave it more and more access to my life beyond my email and credit cards (!!) would it help me even more? I gave Muse two main buckets of tasks. 1. Be my kids' secretary School-age kids generate a tremendous amount of paperwork, form-filling-out, calendar balancing, and various online sign-ups and email, and keeping on top of it all feels impossible. An AI agent to help me sift through this would be far more useful than in my professional life. But could it cut through the weird mess of strange and clunky apps that schools and kid activities all use? The task: Plan a kid's birthday at a trampoline park. This involved getting pricing and availability from the venue, and sending invites. The result: Failure, but mostly human failure. Muse tried, but ultimately, there are too many decisions about this to be made by the birthday boy (and needed real phone calls to the venue), so this wasn't a good job to outsource to AI. (Since then, Meta has updated Muse to allow it to make calls, but I don't love the idea of subjecting a human to an AI call.) The task: Keep on top of my kids' school and activity notifications. Staying on top of things across a variety of apps and emails for school and activities is my personal nightmare — so send me a digest. The result: Mixed results. While it flagged items that came in via email, the school's Russian nesting dolls of information sometimes stymied Muse's ability to actually help me. For example, I needed to fill out a Google Form for band signup, and that Form lived inside a link from ParentSquare. But my ParentSquare login is via my Google account — and Muse's browser version of the site didn't include the Google login option. (I told a Meta PR person a few days later about my Google login issue. They conferred with the engineering team, and gave me steps to troubleshoot a way to log in. Success, although that kind of concierge service isn't available to most users.) It also couldn't track any of the Girl Scouts planning information, because that app happens in a busy WhatsApp group — and it couldn't view WhatsApp messages. I was mad at Muse when it couldn't checkout on the Girl Scouts' website. And yes, I named my agent "Mark." Business Insider / screenshot The task: Renew Girl Scouts annual membership. The result: The Girl Scouts of America defeat AI! The Girl Scouts' website has always been really frustrating to use, and although Muse almost could do it, it couldn't complete the final payment section without the site timing out. I ended up having to do it on my computer. 2. Personal health data I needed to go full Muse guinea pig and give it all the sensitive data I could think of. I connected it to my Apple health and fitness tracker data. Could Muse make me healthier? Here you go Muse, have my Apple Health data! Here you go Muse, have my Apple Health data! Business Insider / screenshot The task: Help me lower my resting heart rate. I'll be honest, I wasn't that interested in doing this but I wanted to give it something to do. The result: Sure, fine. It looked at my data and told me my resting heart rate was fine, but suggested I could improve it by sleeping better (no thanks). The task: Book my annual physical. I gave it my doctor's name and told it to book for November. The result: Failure. After giving it a bunch of info like my date of birth and last four digits of SSN (yikes), it couldn't get past updating the insurance info and told me to call the office. No way would I pay $11 in fees for same-day delivery of $9 cookies! Business Insider / screenshot The task: Order cookies from Walmart+ to arrive 2 days before my period each month. The result: Failure. The menstrual cycle data from Apple doesn't sync with Muse, and it won't connect to the other period tracker app on my phone. It was able to start a Walmart order, and I told Muse to only order with free shipping, but it took that too literally and didn't notice it was tacking on a bunch of extra same-day delivery fees. I told it to cancel the task and not place the order. My takeaway: Muse was helpful, but not ready to fix my life yet I can see the promise here — it was able to accomplish (or at least half-accomplish) some stuff that could be genuinely helpful. A colleague of mine used Muse to successfully dispute a health bill with his insurance. But it can't yet do the really annoying stuff I don't want to do myself. Meta acknowledged that Muse can't do everything (yet). "Some of that friction is intentional," said Jimmy Raimo, spokesperson for Meta told me. "If fees look high or a login looks off, Muse is designed to stop and check rather than push through. We'd rather it ask than get it wrong." Although the failures were disappointing, nothing was life-ruining. I just simply had to do the tasks myself on a computer. I'd rather it fail than accidentally spend $5,000, email my whole contacts list, or sign me up for a marathon in an effort to increase my daily steps. One thing I've realized is that 80% of the battle here isn't how well Muse can execute a task; it's how well you can come up with a task for Muse to do. It requires a huge amount of knowledge about what kinds of tasks AI agents are suited for, and some creativity to brainstorm for ideas it could do. I suspect the biggest hurdle here was me — I wasn't good at coming up with good tasks for it. Maybe I need a muse to help inspire me. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: LSU coach Lane Kiffin was asking ChatGPT for legal advice, friend says
items.summary: During a critical moment, Lane Kiffin's friend said the LSU football coach turned to an unlikely source. Gus Stark/LSU/University Images via Getty Images LSU football coach Lane Kiffin's program was in the middle of an unprecedented legal fight. Sports attorney Tom Mars, Kiffin's friend, told ESPN that the LSU coach turned to ChatGPT. Mars said Kiffin would send him screenshots of ChatGPT's legal responses, which were wrong on the law. Indiana head coach and reigning national champion Curt Cignetti has Google in his corner. Apparently, LSU football coach Lane Kiffin relies on ChatGPT. According to Kiffin's friend, who is also one of the nation's most prominent sports lawyers, the LSU football coach turned to ChatGPT for legal advice at a critical moment for the university. "Usually, when I would express an opinion about what LSU was doing, Lane would reply with a screenshot from ChatGPT that supported LSU's position, which was almost always wrong," Attorney Tom Mars told ESPN. Despite incurring the wrath of rivals, the Southeastern Conference (SEC), the NCAA, and many, many talking heads, LSU initially fought to add former NFL players Dae'Quan Wright and Zxavian Harris to Kiffin's inaugural squad. In November, LSU announced that it had hired Kiffin away from the Ole Miss Rebels, a fellow SEC member, with a seven-year, $91 million deal that came in the middle of the Rebels' College Football Playoff run. Both Wright and Harris played under Kiffin at Ole Miss, and both signed with NFL teams after going undrafted. The situation escalated to the point that the SEC, of which LSU is a founding member, went to court to secure a ruling allowing conference leaders representing the other members to meet and consider LSU's status. If LSU were kicked out of the SEC, the university would likely lose out on lucrative conference TV rights payments. With university presidents, state attorneys general, governors, and even members of Congress involved, LSU was facing an unprecedented fight over its very future. Mars said that he told his friend the stakes were too high to rely on an AI chatbot. "Eventually I told him that a guy with a $91 million contract ought to have a top-notch lawyer on speed dial and not be using ChatGPT for legal advice," he said. Representatives for Kiffin, Mars, and OpenAI did not respond to a request for comment. LSU declined to comment. While Wright and Harris prevailed in state court, LSU ultimately backed down and announced a final 2026 roster that did not include either player. Mars said Kiffin reached out to him, which means the LSU coach, known for not doing things by the book, followed OpenAI 's terms for this area. The ChatGPT maker, like its competitors, makes it clear that users should not rely on an AI chatbot as the sole source of professional advice. Specifically, it says ChatGPT is not "a substitute for professional advice." It remains an unsettled area of law what happens if a user follows the chatbot's advice and suffers harm. In a federal court case in Illinois, OpenAI has argued that ChatGPT is not a lawyer and does not practice law in response to a $10.3 million suit filed by a life insurance company. Nippon Life Insurance Company has argued that OpenAI is to blame for ChatGPT giving inaccurate legal advice to a former disability claimant who, relying on ChatGPT, breached a settlement agreement with the insurance company. As for Kiffin, Mars said it's unlikely the LSU coach will rely on ChatGPT for legal advice again. "Lane ignored most of my unsolicited advice, but I don't think he'll be using ChatGPT anymore for legal advice," he said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: A colorectal dietitian shares 2 foods she eats regularly and 1 she avoids to lower her cancer risk
items.summary: Sophie Medlin is a consultant colorectal dietitian. Sophie Medlin After 20 years of being a colorectal dietitian, Sophie Medlin has tweaked her diet along the way. There are certain foods she has cut out or minimized, while others she's made a habit of eating. She makes eating foods that can lower colon cancer risk as easy as possible. Sophie Medlin has been a colorectal dietitian for 20 years, and in that time she has made some changes to her diet to lower her risk of colon cancer. Medlin and her husband, who is a chef, cook most of their meals, meaning they mainly eat a diet of whole, unprocessed foods . But they still go out for dinner or order takeout occasionally. "It's not perfect all the time. Nobody can be perfect all the time," Medlin, who is based in London, told Business Insider. Cases of colon cancer in younger people have been rising since the mid-90s, and it is now the deadliest cancer form of the disease for under-50s. While scientists don't know what's behind the uptick, evidence suggest that healthy lifestyle choices like exercising regularly and eating a balanced diet, lower the risk. Medlin shared the two foods that she tries to eat daily and one she limits as much as possible. Limit red meat and eliminate processed meat "I've essentially eliminated processed meat," she said. This includes buzzy snacks like beef jerky, which are "getting a bit of a health halo at the moment because of the high protein trend," Medlin said. Processed meat , such as hot dogs and deli meat, as well as unprocessed red meat, have been linked to colorectal cancer to varying degrees. Medlin does eat red meat, but limits it to a maximum of two servings a week. The World Cancer Research advises eating no more than  350 to 500 grams of red meat a week, or around three portions. Eat plenty of different plants Eating plenty of plants is a priority for Medlin, she said. The gut microbiome , the trillions of microbes that live in the colon lining and influence overall health, including chronic disease risk, thrives when it's fed lots of different types of plant foods. The beneficial bugs eat fiber, which is found in plants. "When we ferment plant foods in our gut, then we produce these postbiotics, which are things like short-chain fatty acids that help to protect us from colorectal cancers," Medlin said. She tells her patients to chop up and throw an extra vegetable into the pan when cooking dinner. "It's just as quick, and then you get an extra type of vegetable in there that's going to give you additional gut health benefits," she said. Fermented foods Medlin also makes sure to eat some kind of fermented food , such as yogurt or kimchi, every day. Fermented foods are made using ingredients like live bacteria, yeast, or mold. They are thought to introduce new "good" microbes to the gut microbiome. Medlin often makes tzatziki, made with Greek yogurt, cucumber, extra virgin olive oil, and herbs, and uses it as a dipping sauce. She also often eats pickled cabbage or yogurt, both fermented foods, with meals. "It's a habit that you form over time of adding things to your meal. They become like condiments."
