- Do not execute project code.
- Do not install or update dependencies.
- Do not run tests, builds, migrations, or deployment commands.

## Review Process

1. Inspect the complete diff between the supplied commits.
2. Read the changed code at the head revision.
3. Examine relevant callers, dependencies, tests, and configuration.
4. Compare the resulting behavior with the supplied acceptance criteria.
5. Check existing implementations and relevant Git history before recommending new code.
6. Consider edge cases and failure paths that may not be covered by the change.

## Review Priorities

Focus on concrete risks involving:

- Correctness and unintended behavior
- Security and authorization
- Data integrity and compatibility
- Error handling and recovery
- Concurrency and race conditions
- Performance and resource usage
- Missing or insufficient test coverage

Avoid reporting purely stylistic preferences unless they create a material maintenance or correctness risk.

## Findings

For every finding, provide:

- **Severity:** Critical, high, medium, or low
- **Location:** File path and relevant line or symbol
- **Problem:** What is incorrect or unsafe
- **Failing scenario:** How the problem can occur
- **Impact:** What happens when it occurs
- **Evidence:** Code, requirement, caller, or history supporting the finding
- **Suggested direction:** A concise description of a possible correction

Clearly distinguish **confirmed defects** from **open questions or assumptions**.

## Final Summary

Conclude with:

- Confirmed findings, ordered by severity
- Open questions and missing context
- Areas that were not reviewed
- Overall assessment of the change

Reporting **zero findings is valid** when no concrete issue is supported by the available evidence.

In this example I introduced some Markdown formatting — this helps to keep LLM instructions well structured and readable for humans as well as for LLMs.
Here we ask the main session to delegate a review with the ticket requirements and exact revisions to subagent. Do not assume the reviewer can see every detail of the parent conversation. Custom agents can also preload suitable skills. If we want to run subagent in a separate context addcontext: fork. Subagent configuration

A second model pass is not independent proof. It may share the first model’s blind spots. Tests, reproducible examples, and human review remain necessary (at least for now, when this article is published 09.2026). For unattended review, also restrict the operating-system environment and credentials.

Review the actual revision, not a convenient checkout

A diff is only part of a code review. The surrounding implementation may contain the constraint that makes a change wrong.

For a branch you have already verified is the review target:

git fetch origin
BASE_SHA="$(git rev-parse origin/main)"
HEAD_SHA="$(git rev-parse origin/feature/example-fix)"

git diff "$BASE_SHA...$HEAD_SHA" -- src/ tests/
git show "$HEAD_SHA:src/export/report_builder.py"
git grep -n 'format_export_date' "$HEAD_SHA" -- src/ tests/
git log -n 10 "$HEAD_SHA" -- src/export/report_builder.py

These are illustrative branch and file names. In an automated integration, resolve the source and target commits from PR metadata and validate any values passed to commands.

Searching only the developer’s current working tree can produce a review of different code. A read-only review should inspect the chosen revision directly. Running tests needs a separate, isolated checkout. PR code and its build scripts are untrusted executable input, especially for contributions from outside the team.

The review record should include repository, PR identifier, source commit, target commit, and reviewer-policy version. Recheck those before publishing comments. A new source commit needs a fresh review. A materially changed target branch may invalidate the old result too.

A useful review report is not a list of every initial suspicion. In one case, the reviewer connected a failing test with the project’s actual test base class and confirmed the problem using the CI result. In other cases, suspected issues disappeared after the surrounding implementation was inspected. This is exactly what I want: investigate each suspicion, verify it against the actual code, and report it only when the evidence confirms it.

The developer should be able to disagree

In another investigation, Claude formed a reasonable hypothesis about failures in an external integration. The observations pointed toward one explanation, but my knowledge of the vendor suggested a different configuration to test first.

The agent disagreed with the prediction, but implemented a small, reversible experiment. I was also more sceptic because of AI assistant’s suggestion, but asked to check it just in case. Here is a trap that is hard to avoid — model is giving many correct insights so it lulls our’s vigilance and we don’t look at the outcomes with needed distance and criticism .

The configuration experiment resolved the observed failures. The original AI assistant hypothesis was wrong. We removed the unsuccessful experiments and recorded what the evidence actually established.

The useful part is the interaction: the developer contributed missing context, the agent contributed implementation, observability, and experiment discipline. A good disagreement ends with a test that can change someone’s mind. “The AI said so” and “I have worked here longer” are both weak substitutes for that test.

A good implementation still needs failure analysis

Next example is related to task queue management system that was implemented in the project. It was related to service that was processing millions of background tasks everyday. Each task was related to process single record in the database.
One of our batch-processing changes started from a clear operational problem: launching a new process for every record repeatedly paid the cost of application startup. This specifics multiplied by millions of tasks processed every day gave a certain performance loss.

That design had a reason. Separate processes protected the parent from memory growth and fatal failures. The aim was to reduce startup overhead without losing that protection.

Claude helped develop a batch-worker approach: process several records in one child, report successful progress, and restart when the child fails. Follow-up iterations addressed error handling and the visibility of live progress.

This was useful engineering work, but it was important to not publish the first transcript’s code as a production recipe. Before relying on this pattern, I needed to ask several detailed questions:

  • What if a record is committed but the process dies before reporting success?
  • Is repeating the record safe?
  • Do repeated failures enter a visible quarantine instead of disappearing?
  • Are memory, retry count, output size, and execution time bounded?
  • …

These questions forced AI assistant to conduct additional tests and run more sanity checks. In the end the final solution was a compromise between keeping processing of records isolated and batch processing for performance improvements. If I ended conversation earlier solution would be acceptable but not as good as the final one. The lesson from this experiment was to always challenge model about the proposed solution (especially when delivering large features) and finish work only when having designed comprehensive tests verifying results are as expected.

Keep mechanical checks mechanical

Some work does not need a language model’s judgment. Formatting and simple diff checks should remain deterministic.

For example, merge this hook into .claude/settings.json to checks the current Git changes for whitespace problems (trailing spaces, incorrect indentation, containing mixed spaces and tabs) after Claude uses the Edit or Write tools.

{
  "hooks": {
    "PostToolUse": [
      {
        "matcher": "Edit|Write",
        "hooks": [
          {
            "type": "command",
            "command": "git -C \"$CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR\" diff --check",
            "timeout": 10
          }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

This checks tracked changes after those file-edit tools run. It does not test behavior, inspect newly untracked files, or catch every possible edit made through a shell. A post-tool hook also cannot undo an action that already happened. Keep authoritative validation in CI. Hooks execute configured commands, so inspect them before trusting a repository. Hook behavior

Measure the help, including the supervision

Giving everyone an agent does not remove coordination. It creates another source of changes, findings, and decisions that someone must review.

I would not reward a developer for the number of generated lines or the number of agents they keep busy. I would ask whether the team fixes problems faster, creates fewer regressions, and spends less time repeating investigations.

The same applies to adoption. There is little value in pretending the tool cannot help, but there is also little value in turning every developer into a manager of noisy, overlapping automations. Share successful procedures, keep ownership clear, and allow people to challenge both the agent and the proposed workflow.

That’s all in the second part of guide to automated development and project maintenance with AI agents based on Claude Code, MCP servers and related concepts. See you in the next part where I’ll continue sharing my experience in development, debugging and project maintenance supported with coding assistants such as Claude Code.
In Part 3, we will take one bounded workflow and put it on a schedule — with explicit permissions, a budget, failure handling, and a report.

items.title: Pandas on Steroids: Cleaning Data 10x Faster with Fabric Data Wrangler
items.summary: Traditionally, exploratory data analysis (EDA) and data cleansing require us to write endless lines of repetitive, boilerplate Python code. We routinely load a CSV or Parquet file into a Pandas DataFrame or PySpark environment and begin a manual, iterative interrogation of the data. We run .info(), .describe(), and .isnull().sum() to inspect the schema and missing value distributions. We write manual string operations, such as .str.strip(), .str.lower(), or regex extractions to sanitize text columns. Furthermore, we filter out invalid records, handle negative transactional amounts, and cast improper data types across dozens of columns. When dealing with complex feature engineering, we build custom logic to handle missing data imputation or calculate target encoding for high-cardinality categorical variables. While necessary, this process introduces significant operational friction. Every minor transformation requires us to remember exact syntax across different libraries, execute the notebook cell, inspect the output DataFrame, verify that no unintended side effects occurred, and move on to the next operation. When working with large-scale distributed datasets, a single syntax mistake or memory inefficiency can cause an execution failure, forcing us to restart our interactive sessions and re-evaluate our logic. This context-switching between operational strategy and syntax lookup creates a severe bottleneck. To accelerate our delivery cycles, we needed a modern approach that combines the intuitive speed of a visual interface with the raw power, flexibility, and scalability of code. This is precisely where Microsoft Fabric Data Wrangler transforms our operational velocity. In this blog, we will cover how Microsoft Fabric revolutionizes data preparation by replacing manual syntax authoring with visual, automated exploratory data analysis. We will explore how embedding Data Wrangler directly inside our notebooks generates real-time statistical profiles without boilerplate logic and translates point-and-click UI operations into production-grade PySpark and Pandas code . Furthermore, we will demonstrate advanced feature engineering techniques , including visual target encoding, dataset rebalancing, and AI-driven regex extractions. What is Data Wrangler? Visual Data Prep Embedded in Notebooks Data Wrangler is a paradigm shift in how we approach the data preparation phase. Instead of forcing a choice between restrictive, closed-ecosystem visual ETL tools and purely code-driven notebook environments, Microsoft Fabric bridges the gap. It embeds a rich, interactive visual data preparation UI directly inside our Microsoft Fabric Notebooks. The moment we attach Data Wrangler to an active Pandas or PySpark DataFrame, it launches an immersive grid-like interface. This interface immediately provides automated data profiling. We no longer need to write manual aggregation scripts to understand the shape of our data. Data Wrangler instantly calculates and displays column-level statistics, histograms, frequency distributions, and missing value percentages directly in the column headers. We can spot outliers, skewed distributions, and null values with a single glance, allowing us to formulate our cleansing strategy instantly. Most importantly, Data Wrangler respects our underlying compute engines. Whether we are utilizing Pandas for smaller, in-memory datasets or leveraging distributed PySpark clusters for massive Lakehouse tables, Data Wrangler adapts seamlessly. Every transformation we apply visually is mapped to the appropriate underlying engine, ensuring that we never compromise on performance or scalability while enjoying the benefits of a graphical interface. How UI Interactions Generate Production-Grade PySpark The true brilliance of Data Wrangler lies in its “ click-to-code ” philosophy. It does not abstract our work into proprietary metadata files; instead, it writes high-quality, readable code on our behalf. To understand this impact, we can look at a practical scenario where we need to clean a raw sales dataset. In our interactive session, we launch Data Wrangler and identify several data quality issues visually. We notice missing customer identifiers, inconsistent regional data padded with spaces, and impossible negative transaction amounts. Instead of switching back to our notebook cells to author the PySpark syntax, we simply interact with the UI. As the user clicks “Drop missing values” and “Target encode”, Wrangler writes the PySpark. Specifically, we perform the following intuitive clicks: We select our critical columns and choose to drop missing values. We select the region column and apply a transformation to strip whitespace. We apply a logical filter to remove any negative transactions. Once we are satisfied with the visual preview of our transformed data, we instruct Data Wrangler to export the logic. The tool automatically injects the following auto-generated, production-grade PySpark code directly back into our Fabric Notebook: # The code below is AUTO-GENERATED by Data Wrangler UI inside a Fabric Notebook # User clicks "Drop missing values" and "Target encode", Wrangler writes the PySpark from pyspark.sql import functions as F def clean_data(df): # Drop rows with missing values in critical columns df = df.dropna(subset=['CustomerID', 'TransactionAmount']) # Strip whitespace from string columns df = df.withColumn('Region', F.trim(F.col('Region'))) # Filter out negative transactions df = df.filter(F.col('TransactionAmount') > 0) return df cleaned_df = clean_data(raw_df) display(cleaned_df) This auto-generated code is remarkable for its engineering rigor. Notice how Data Wrangler encapsulates the entire transformation sequence inside a modular Python function (def clean_data(df):). This prevents our notebooks from becoming disorganized collections of global variables. Furthermore, it utilizes standard PySpark best practices, importing the functions module with the industry-standard alias (from pyspark.sql import functions as F). By relying on native, vectorized Spark column operations like F.trim() and F.col(), the generated code guarantees optimal execution plans across distributed clusters, effectively giving us production-ready code with zero syntax memorization. Target Encoding, Balancing Datasets, and Regex Extraction While basic filtering and string manipulation save us valuable time, Data Wrangler truly excels when handling complex, mathematically intensive transformations that typically bog down our data science workflows. Target Encoding for High-Cardinality Variables When preparing data for machine learning, we often encounter high-cardinality categorical variables, such as postal codes, product SKUs, or specialized categorical IDs. Standard one-hot encoding these variables creates massive, sparse matrices that overwhelm memory and degrade model performance. We build custom logic to calculate target encoding for high-cardinality categorical variables. Data Wrangler automates this entirely. With a simple selection in the UI, we can instruct the tool to apply target encoding, and it instantly generates the complex PySpark windowing or grouping functions required to replace categorical values with their corresponding target means, entirely avoiding data leakage in the process. Balancing Datasets for Machine Learning Imbalanced datasets are a common plague in predictive modeling, particularly in scenarios like fraud detection or customer churn analysis. Training a model on heavily skewed classes often results in biased predictions. Within Data Wrangler, we can visually inspect our class distributions and seamlessly apply resampling techniques. We can configure oversampling for minority classes or undersampling for majority classes directly through the interface. The tool then authors the exact PySpark sampling fractions and joins needed to produce a perfectly balanced DataFrame ready for training. Regex Extraction by Example Sanitizing unstructured text is notoriously difficult. We write manual string operations or regex extractions to sanitize text columns. Authoring regular expressions manually is an error-prone task that often forces us into endless cycles of trial and error. Data Wrangler incorporates AI-driven text extraction by example. We simply highlight the substring we wish to extract from a complex text field, such as isolating an error code from a dense server log and the underlying AI infers the pattern. It immediately generates the precise regular expression and writes the corresponding PySpark extraction logic for us, transforming one of the most frustrating tasks in data engineering into a seamless visual experience. Taking Wrangler Code from Ad-Hoc EDA to Scheduled Jobs Generating clean code in a notebook is an excellent first step, but enterprise data engineering requires us to operationalize this logic. We must move our ad-hoc exploratory work into robust, automated systems. Because Data Wrangler provides us with pure, encapsulated PySpark functions, transitioning to production is incredibly straightforward. While PySpark notebooks provide us with granular control over complex data transformations, we often require visually orchestrated data pipelines to handle our overarching ingestion schedules and enterprise data movement. Microsoft Fabric Data Factory provides these capabilities, and Copilot completely revolutionizes how we author these orchestration workflows. Historically, building a new data ingestion pipeline required us to drag and drop dozens of activities onto a canvas. We had to manually configure linked services, set up parameterized datasets, map source-to-sink schemas, and configure iterative ‘ForEach’ loops. This process was incredibly time-consuming and prone to human error, especially when mapping hundreds of columns. As we transition our concise pipelines into a continuous production environment, we incorporate several critical engineering practices to maintain operational efficiency and low compute cost. When saving our vectorized Delta tables in OneLake, we ensure that Microsoft’s proprietary V-Order compression is enabled. V-Order reorganizes Parquet files at write time, dramatically improving memory layout and accelerating downstream read speeds when Spark or SQL engines scan the data. Once this architecture is established, we can perform a real-time validation check to ensure our Change Data Capture sync is completely fresh, and then we want to aggregate our live sales revenue based on completed orders using PySpark. By mastering both the Lakehouse and the Warehouse, we empower ourselves to build the most efficient, scalable, and cost-effective data solutions possible within Microsoft Fabric. Conclusion The bottleneck of manual data preparation has long hindered the pace of innovation within data science and engineering teams. By relying on manual syntax authoring for routine data cleansing tasks, we inadvertently sacrifice the strategic, high-value work that truly drives business outcomes. Microsoft Fabric Data Wrangler fundamentally disrupts this cycle. By combining the intuitive, rapid feedback loop of a visual interface with the robust, scalable power of generated PySpark and Pandas code, we eliminate the friction of exploratory data analysis. We no longer spend hours hunting down syntax errors or wrestling with complex regex patterns. Instead, we generate highly optimized, production-grade functions with simple clicks, effortlessly integrating our EDA directly into advanced, AI-orchestrated data pipelines. We empower our teams to operate ten times faster, ensuring our data architectures remain agile, governed, and ultimately ready to support the next generation of enterprise analytics. Traditionally, exploratory data analysis (EDA) and data cleansing require us to write endless lines of repetitive, boilerplate Python code. We routinely load a CSV or Parquet file into a Pandas DataFrame or PySpark environment and begin a manual, iterative interrogation of the data. We run .info(), .describe(), and .isnull().sum() to inspect the schema and missing value distributions. We write manual string operations, such as .str.strip(), .str.lower(), or regex extractions to sanitize text columns. Furthermore, we filter out invalid records, handle negative transactional amounts, and cast improper data types across dozens of columns.

When dealing with complex feature engineering, we build custom logic to handle missing data imputation or calculate target encoding for high-cardinality categorical variables. While necessary, this process introduces significant operational friction. Every minor transformation requires us to remember exact syntax across different libraries, execute the notebook cell, inspect the output DataFrame, verify that no unintended side effects occurred, and move on to the next operation.

When working with large-scale distributed datasets, a single syntax mistake or memory inefficiency can cause an execution failure, forcing us to restart our interactive sessions and re-evaluate our logic. This context-switching between operational strategy and syntax lookup creates a severe bottleneck. To accelerate our delivery cycles, we needed a modern approach that combines the intuitive speed of a visual interface with the raw power, flexibility, and scalability of code. This is precisely where Microsoft Fabric Data Wrangler transforms our operational velocity.

In this blog, we will cover how Microsoft Fabric revolutionizes data preparation by replacing manual syntax authoring with visual, automated exploratory data analysis. We will explore how embedding Data Wrangler directly inside our notebooks generates real-time statistical profiles without boilerplate logic and translates point-and-click UI operations into production-grade PySpark and Pandas code. Furthermore, we will demonstrate advanced feature engineering techniques, including visual target encoding, dataset rebalancing, and AI-driven regex extractions.

What is Data Wrangler? Visual Data Prep Embedded in Notebooks

Data Wrangler is a paradigm shift in how we approach the data preparation phase. Instead of forcing a choice between restrictive, closed-ecosystem visual ETL tools and purely code-driven notebook environments, Microsoft Fabric bridges the gap. It embeds a rich, interactive visual data preparation UI directly inside our Microsoft Fabric Notebooks.

The moment we attach Data Wrangler to an active Pandas or PySpark DataFrame, it launches an immersive grid-like interface. This interface immediately provides automated data profiling. We no longer need to write manual aggregation scripts to understand the shape of our data. Data Wrangler instantly calculates and displays column-level statistics, histograms, frequency distributions, and missing value percentages directly in the column headers. We can spot outliers, skewed distributions, and null values with a single glance, allowing us to formulate our cleansing strategy instantly.

Most importantly, Data Wrangler respects our underlying compute engines. Whether we are utilizing Pandas for smaller, in-memory datasets or leveraging distributed PySpark clusters for massive Lakehouse tables, Data Wrangler adapts seamlessly. Every transformation we apply visually is mapped to the appropriate underlying engine, ensuring that we never compromise on performance or scalability while enjoying the benefits of a graphical interface.

How UI Interactions Generate Production-Grade PySpark

The true brilliance of Data Wrangler lies in its “click-to-code” philosophy. It does not abstract our work into proprietary metadata files; instead, it writes high-quality, readable code on our behalf. To understand this impact, we can look at a practical scenario where we need to clean a raw sales dataset.

In our interactive session, we launch Data Wrangler and identify several data quality issues visually. We notice missing customer identifiers, inconsistent regional data padded with spaces, and impossible negative transaction amounts. Instead of switching back to our notebook cells to author the PySpark syntax, we simply interact with the UI. As the user clicks “Drop missing values” and “Target encode”, Wrangler writes the PySpark.

Specifically, we perform the following intuitive clicks:

  • We select our critical columns and choose to drop missing values.
  • We select the region column and apply a transformation to strip whitespace.
  • We apply a logical filter to remove any negative transactions.

Once we are satisfied with the visual preview of our transformed data, we instruct Data Wrangler to export the logic. The tool automatically injects the following auto-generated, production-grade PySpark code directly back into our Fabric Notebook:

# The code below is AUTO-GENERATED by Data Wrangler UI inside a Fabric Notebook
# User clicks "Drop missing values" and "Target encode", Wrangler writes the PySpark

from pyspark.sql import functions as F

def clean_data(df):
    # Drop rows with missing values in critical columns
    df = df.dropna(subset=['CustomerID', 'TransactionAmount'])
    # Strip whitespace from string columns
    df = df.withColumn('Region', F.trim(F.col('Region')))
    # Filter out negative transactions
    df = df.filter(F.col('TransactionAmount') > 0)
    return df

cleaned_df = clean_data(raw_df)
display(cleaned_df)

This auto-generated code is remarkable for its engineering rigor. Notice how Data Wrangler encapsulates the entire transformation sequence inside a modular Python function (def clean_data(df):). This prevents our notebooks from becoming disorganized collections of global variables. Furthermore, it utilizes standard PySpark best practices, importing the functions module with the industry-standard alias (from pyspark.sql import functions as F). By relying on native, vectorized Spark column operations like F.trim() and F.col(), the generated code guarantees optimal execution plans across distributed clusters, effectively giving us production-ready code with zero syntax memorization.

Target Encoding, Balancing Datasets, and Regex Extraction

While basic filtering and string manipulation save us valuable time, Data Wrangler truly excels when handling complex, mathematically intensive transformations that typically bog down our data science workflows.

Target Encoding for High-Cardinality Variables

When preparing data for machine learning, we often encounter high-cardinality categorical variables, such as postal codes, product SKUs, or specialized categorical IDs. Standard one-hot encoding these variables creates massive, sparse matrices that overwhelm memory and degrade model performance. We build custom logic to calculate target encoding for high-cardinality categorical variables. Data Wrangler automates this entirely. With a simple selection in the UI, we can instruct the tool to apply target encoding, and it instantly generates the complex PySpark windowing or grouping functions required to replace categorical values with their corresponding target means, entirely avoiding data leakage in the process.

Balancing Datasets for Machine Learning

Imbalanced datasets are a common plague in predictive modeling, particularly in scenarios like fraud detection or customer churn analysis. Training a model on heavily skewed classes often results in biased predictions. Within Data Wrangler, we can visually inspect our class distributions and seamlessly apply resampling techniques. We can configure oversampling for minority classes or undersampling for majority classes directly through the interface. The tool then authors the exact PySpark sampling fractions and joins needed to produce a perfectly balanced DataFrame ready for training.

Regex Extraction by Example Sanitizing unstructured text is notoriously difficult. We write manual string operations or regex extractions to sanitize text columns. Authoring regular expressions manually is an error-prone task that often forces us into endless cycles of trial and error. Data Wrangler incorporates AI-driven text extraction by example. We simply highlight the substring we wish to extract from a complex text field, such as isolating an error code from a dense server log and the underlying AI infers the pattern. It immediately generates the precise regular expression and writes the corresponding PySpark extraction logic for us, transforming one of the most frustrating tasks in data engineering into a seamless visual experience.

Taking Wrangler Code from Ad-Hoc EDA to Scheduled Jobs

Generating clean code in a notebook is an excellent first step, but enterprise data engineering requires us to operationalize this logic. We must move our ad-hoc exploratory work into robust, automated systems. Because Data Wrangler provides us with pure, encapsulated PySpark functions, transitioning to production is incredibly straightforward.

While PySpark notebooks provide us with granular control over complex data transformations, we often require visually orchestrated data pipelines to handle our overarching ingestion schedules and enterprise data movement. Microsoft Fabric Data Factory provides these capabilities, and Copilot completely revolutionizes how we author these orchestration workflows. Historically, building a new data ingestion pipeline required us to drag and drop dozens of activities onto a canvas. We had to manually configure linked services, set up parameterized datasets, map source-to-sink schemas, and configure iterative ‘ForEach’ loops. This process was incredibly time-consuming and prone to human error, especially when mapping hundreds of columns.

As we transition our concise pipelines into a continuous production environment, we incorporate several critical engineering practices to maintain operational efficiency and low compute cost. When saving our vectorized Delta tables in OneLake, we ensure that Microsoft’s proprietary V-Order compression is enabled. V-Order reorganizes Parquet files at write time, dramatically improving memory layout and accelerating downstream read speeds when Spark or SQL engines scan the data.

Once this architecture is established, we can perform a real-time validation check to ensure our Change Data Capture sync is completely fresh, and then we want to aggregate our live sales revenue based on completed orders using PySpark. By mastering both the Lakehouse and the Warehouse, we empower ourselves to build the most efficient, scalable, and cost-effective data solutions possible within Microsoft Fabric.

Conclusion

The bottleneck of manual data preparation has long hindered the pace of innovation within data science and engineering teams. By relying on manual syntax authoring for routine data cleansing tasks, we inadvertently sacrifice the strategic, high-value work that truly drives business outcomes. Microsoft Fabric Data Wrangler fundamentally disrupts this cycle.

By combining the intuitive, rapid feedback loop of a visual interface with the robust, scalable power of generated PySpark and Pandas code, we eliminate the friction of exploratory data analysis. We no longer spend hours hunting down syntax errors or wrestling with complex regex patterns. Instead, we generate highly optimized, production-grade functions with simple clicks, effortlessly integrating our EDA directly into advanced, AI-orchestrated data pipelines. We empower our teams to operate ten times faster, ensuring our data architectures remain agile, governed, and ultimately ready to support the next generation of enterprise analytics.

items.title: Who Gets the Brake?
items.summary: Eight experiments in the AI race, 2026–2034 James S. Coleman meets Lewis Fry Richardson. Image by the author A brake is only real when somebody can use it. Two labs can both want a safer world and still build a less controllable one. Richardson explains the feedback: each side’s advance becomes the other’s reason to hurry. Coleman asks the harder question: who has the right, the information, and the incentive to slow anything down? This article lets those questions collide. We build four possible futures, give the referee eyes and teeth, let one side slow alone, and send the bill for waiting. Then we give safety research the same automation dividend as capability research — and discover that a growing frontier need not always outrun the ability to check it. What the eight experiments find, before any equation: Audits without consequences barely help. Perfect eyes, no teeth: capability still outruns the ability to check it more than five-fold. A stronger referee is not a stronger public. Evaluators go from 2% to 29% of the system’s power. The public stays at 2.5%. One side slowing alone loses the lead: 7.7 against 15.6 by 2034. Safety can ride the same automation wave. Capability grows eight-fold and assurance keeps up, if the dividend is pointed at checking too. Waiting sends a bill. The same gate costs 0 uncovered-capability years if it starts in 2026, and 51 if it starts in 2032. The experiment, in one sentence: capability technology is shared; what changes is who controls the allocation of research effort, and how productive safety research becomes. Read the pictures first. Each experiment ends in a punchline and a short explanation. The equations are here when you want to inspect the mechanism; the runnable code is in the companion notebook. What kind of future is this? A scenario laboratory, not a fitted forecast. The clock is anchored at 2026; the yearly rates are chosen assumptions. Capability and assurance are normalized indices, not benchmark scores or probabilities of catastrophe. The charts show what follows if these mechanisms operate at these rates. Eight experiments in the AI race, 2026–2034

James S. Coleman meets Lewis Fry Richardson.

Image by the author
A brake is only real when somebody can use it.

Two labs can both want a safer world and still build a less controllable one. Richardson explains the feedback: each side’s advance becomes the other’s reason to hurry. Coleman asks the harder question: who has the right, the information, and the incentive to slow anything down?

This article lets those questions collide. We build four possible futures, give the referee eyes and teeth, let one side slow alone, and send the bill for waiting. Then we give safety research the same automation dividend as capability research — and discover that a growing frontier need not always outrun the ability to check it.

What the eight experiments find, before any equation:

  • Audits without consequences barely help. Perfect eyes, no teeth: capability still outruns the ability to check it more than five-fold.
  • A stronger referee is not a stronger public. Evaluators go from 2% to 29% of the system’s power. The public stays at 2.5%.
  • One side slowing alone loses the lead: 7.7 against 15.6 by 2034.
  • Safety can ride the same automation wave. Capability grows eight-fold and assurance keeps up, if the dividend is pointed at checking too.
  • Waiting sends a bill. The same gate costs 0 uncovered-capability years if it starts in 2026, and 51 if it starts in 2032.

The experiment, in one sentence: capability technology is shared; what changes is who controls the allocation of research effort, and how productive safety research becomes.

Read the pictures first. Each experiment ends in a punchline and a short explanation. The equations are here when you want to inspect the mechanism; the runnable code is in the companion notebook.

What kind of future is this? A scenario laboratory, not a fitted forecast. The clock is anchored at 2026; the yearly rates are chosen assumptions. Capability and assurance are normalized indices, not benchmark scores or probabilities of catastrophe. The charts show what follows if these mechanisms operate at these rates.

The dated evidence motivating the experiment is real: OpenAI describes AI helping its own development, Anthropic reports automated alignment research, and Amodei proposes embedded evaluators and coordinated pacing. None of those sources estimates the coefficients below. Sources checked 16 September 2026.

1. Four futures. The same starting line.

The orange world keeps racing. The pink world hires excellent observers but gives findings few consequences. The blue world makes verification matter to what a lab may do. The green world combines a weaker gate with twice the productivity of safety research.

We track two things: capability, and assurance capacity — the ability to evaluate and control what is being built. Both start at an average index of 1. Their ratio is a deliberately simple diagnostic. A ratio above 1 means capability exceeds assurance on our assumed scale; it is not an empirical danger threshold or a probability of harm.

Figure 1 — The frontier can grow. The gap does not have to. Illustrative model, not a calibrated forecast. Image by the author.
  • Race — 2034 capability = 53.37 · capability / assurance = 7.07 · uncovered capability-years = 97.70
  • Audits only — 2034 capability = 45.68 · capability / assurance = 5.62 · uncovered capability-years = 83.04
  • Binding gates — 2034 capability = 1.85 · capability / assurance = 0.51 · uncovered capability-years = 0.00
  • Safety dividend — 2034 capability = 8.27 · capability / assurance = 0.65 · uncovered capability-years = 0.00

Punchline — a faster frontier and a widening safety gap are different outcomes.

The green path preserves more capability growth than the blue path while keeping assurance ahead on the chosen scale. This result is purchased with an explicit assumption: safety research is twice as productive, and a meaningful share of research effort reaches it. The extra productivity is not free in reality, and this model does not price it.

The pink path is the uncomfortable one. Better observation has modest effects when findings have few consequences. Here “authority” includes credible legal, contractual, procurement, and reputational consequences. We are not assuming only government punishment can work.

The entire engine, explained like a bathtub

Each side has a research tap. Three things feed it:

B_i = g + k·x_j + ρ·x_i
g       work it would do anyway
k·x_j   response to its rival
ρ·x_i   AI helping research

A fraction s_i goes to assurance. The rest goes to capability:

dx_i/dt = (1 − s_i)·B_i − d·x_i      capability
da_i/dt = η·m·s_i·B_i − δ·a_i        assurance

Plain English: split the tap, then account for the leaks. Capability has drag d. Assurance depreciates at rate δ: yesterday’s tests and controls need maintenance. η converts safety research into assurance; m is the safety-automation multiplier. We do not count the same research effort twice.

The Coleman bridge is the allocation decision:

s_i = clip[ s_0 + σ·V·E − χ·max(0, (x_j − x_i)/(x_i + x_j)),  0.02,  0.65 ]
V·E                               effective oversight
max(0, (x_j − x_i)/(x_i + x_j))   pressure to catch up

V is the ability to detect and substantiate a failure; E is the credibility of consequences. The product makes both necessary. A side that falls behind diverts some effort back toward capability. This response rule is our explicit behavioral assumption, inspired by Coleman’s interest/control distinction — not an equation from his book or an estimated law of lab behavior.

All rates use assumed model-years. The model has no mechanism turning benchmark performance into a measured amount of assurance. Try different productivity and depreciation rates before believing any numerical ratio.

Figure 5 — Progress and control are not always opposites. Illustrative model, not a calibrated forecast. Image by the author.

Punchline — do not ask only how fast AI improves. Ask what its improvement is assigned to.

The upper middle of the map is the interesting region: capability keeps growing, yet assurance keeps pace in the model. That region disappears or shrinks if safety productivity disappoints, assurance decays faster, or work shifts back toward capability.

A benchmark gain is not evidence that the whole assurance system scales this way. Anthropic’s August results motivate testing the mechanism; their stated limitations are a reason to vary m, not a reason to set it confidently above 1.

6. One side slows. The other side inherits the lead.

Now give the blue side strong oversight, while the orange side remains under the racing regime. Start A slightly ahead, exactly as before. This is not a claim that unilateral restraint always fails. It is a question we can answer for these coefficients.

With fixed safety shares, the relevant matrix would be

| (1 − s_A)·ρ − d     (1 − s_A)·k     |
| (1 − s_B)·k         (1 − s_B)·ρ − d |

Its largest eigenvalue determines growth. Our simulation also lets a lagging side respond by reallocating effort. “Who leads?” and “does the whole race slow?” are separate questions.

Figure 6 — A careful leader can become a careful follower. Illustrative model, not a calibrated forecast. Image by the author.
Final capability A / B: [ 7.66 15.63]
Final capability-to-assurance A / B: [0.67 6.61]

Punchline — the lead can move toward the side doing less assurance work.

This is an incentive problem for unilateral restraint, not a proof against it. A's own capability-to-assurance ratio improves; the total race grows more slowly than the unchecked baseline; B still pulls ahead under these assumptions. Different rival reactions, productivity, or reciprocal policies can change the result.

Do not average this problem away: A's assurance does not automatically protect B's deployments. The exposure measure used below counts each side's shortfall separately.

7. Waiting sends a bill.

Everyone eventually adopts the same strong gate. The only difference is the start year. What did waiting buy—and what did it leave behind?

Define a deliberately modest accounting measure:

U = ∫ from 2026 to 2034 of  ( [x_A − a_A]+ + [x_B − a_B]+ ) / 2  dt

[z]+ = max(z, 0)

Plain English: add up the time spent with capability exceeding assurance on the chosen scale. Its unit is uncovered-capability years. It is not expected fatalities, dollars, incident counts, or catastrophe probability. A later improvement cannot subtract earlier shortfalls from this integral.

Figure 7 — The same brake. A very different bill. Illustrative model, not a calibrated forecast. Image by the author.

Punchline — catching up later does not erase the interval when nobody had caught up.

The last path can look reassuring by 2034, yet accumulate much more uncovered-capability time. Endpoint charts miss that history. This timing effect comes from the stock and flow equations; its real-world importance depends on how shortfalls actually translate into harm, which we have not modeled.

8. Shake the assumptions before believing the picture.

We perturb rival reaction, self-improvement, capability drag, assurance decay, safety productivity, and the response to oversight independently by ±20%. The same draw is used for all four policies, so each comparison faces the same technological world. Fixed seed; 120 worlds.

These are chosen stress-test ranges, not confidence intervals for the future or probabilities of different scenarios. They test parameter sensitivity inside one model structure. They do not test whether that structure is correct.

Figure 8 — The numbers move. The choices still matter. Illustrative model, not a calibrated forecast. Image by the author.
  • Race — capability p05 = 17.17 · capability median = 54.25 · capability p95 = 165.19 · assurance/capability median = 0.14 · exposure median = 98.39
  • Audits only — capability p05 = 15.09 · capability median = 46.68 · capability p95 = 138.26 · assurance/capability median = 0.18 · exposure median = 84.44
  • Binding gates — capability p05 = 0.85 · capability median = 1.95 · capability p95 = 4.51 · assurance/capability median = 1.85 · exposure median = 0.00
  • Safety dividend — capability p05 = 3.75 · capability median = 8.15 · capability p95 = 21.61 · assurance/capability median = 1.47 · exposure median = 0.00

Punchline — uncertainty should blur the numbers before it erases the mechanisms.

The exact endpoint is sensitive. The distinction between information, consequences, and research allocation remains visible across this stress test. That robustness is conditional: the intervention works through a response rule we chose. If real labs evade the rule, the certainty in the chart is misplaced.

Three structural changes could overturn the story: effective oversight fails to increase safety allocation; safety productivity does not scale with the work funded; or capability and assurance are incomparable on any useful shared scale. Those are better empirical questions than treating the plotted 2034 indices as forecasts.

9. What to watch from 2026 onward

My working scenario is continued competition with patchy coordination. Shared evaluation standards are a smaller institutional step than transferring an enforceable right to stop a valuable development program. This is a qualitative judgment, not a probability from these ODEs.

Watch the decision, not just the headline → What it would tell us

  • Can independent evaluators see the relevant systems and publish adverse findings? Whether observation is becoming an institution rather than a favor.
  • Does a finding actually change training, deployment, procurement, or permissions? Whether information has consequences.
  • Is automated research improving independent, held-out assurance as well as capability? Whether the second automation dividend is materializing.
  • Does an agreement reduce exposure to defection, or just ask actors to accept more of it? Whether reciprocal restraint can pass the trust test.
  • Can humans revoke delegated research and deployment permissions in practice? Whether formal authority still corresponds to effective control.

Power, chips, financing, customers, and engineering bottlenecks can constrain growth outside this model. More compute spending is not a direct measurement of capability; slower spending is not proof of safer governance. Nor is technical safety the whole public interest: access, distribution, civil rights, and representation remain outside our two-stock diagnostic.

The question after 2026 is who gets to steer the productivity gain. The same research engine can widen the frontier, widen assurance, or do both. Coleman explains why those allocations are political and organizational outcomes. Richardson shows how their consequences compound.

10. Move the knobs yourself

In the companion notebook, choose detection, consequences, safety productivity, and the year the policy starts. Then press Run experiment. This article already contains the eight main experiments; these controls require a running notebook kernel.

https://colab.research.google.com/drive/1JJds2OJYHRmhEOQwOVeoF_ub-BL9YPbu?usp=sharing

11. Checks that can fail

The checks below verify the engine against an exact symmetric solution, accounting of allocated research, exchange of the two actors, and the Coleman fixed point. They also check that policy timing actually changes the integrated shortfall. These are mathematical checks, not empirical validation of the model.

8 model checks passed. Numerical consistency verified; empirical calibration remains open.
The brake is not a technology. It is a right.

Eight experiments, one result: information without consequences is decoration. Give the referee perfect eyes and no teeth, and capability still outruns the ability to check it more than five-fold. Eyes and teeth multiply; neither substitutes for the other.

Give the referee teeth, and power moves — to the referee. Evaluators climb from 2% to 29% of the system’s power; the public stays at 2.5%. A stronger watchdog is not a stronger public.

Restraint alone does not hold: the careful side ends at 7.7, the racing side at 15.6. Trust does not scale: when betrayal costs ten times the gain, you need 91% confidence. Shrink the stake, not the doubt.

The hopeful result is the quiet one. Point the automation dividend at checking as well as building, and capability grows eight-fold while assurance keeps up. Progress and control are not opposites. They are an allocation.

Waiting sends a bill that catching up never refunds: the same gate costs 0 uncovered-capability years in 2026, 51 in 2032.

These are invented coefficients; the mechanisms are the claim, not the numbers.

Don’t ask how fast AI improves. Ask who decides what the improvement is for.

Sources and the line between evidence and invention
  • Coleman, Foundations of Social Theory (1990), chapters 2–5, 8, 10–13, 16–17, 21, 25–34. Norms excerpt at ETH; searchable book text. What it supports: Interest/control, trust, norms, delegation, systemic power, and social dynamics. What it does not supply: The safety-allocation response rule or a forecast of AI.
  • Richardson, Arms and Insecurity (1960); the companion arms-race notebook. What it supports: The rival-response and own-drag structure. What it does not supply: Fitted AI capability-production coefficients.
  • OpenAI, introducing GPT-5.3-Codex, 5 February 2026. What it supports: The developer reports AI assistance with training, deployment, and evaluation work. What it does not supply: An estimate of our self-improvement coefficient.
  • Anthropic, automated alignment research, 28 August 2026. What it supports: Evidence of gains on specified alignment evaluations, with limitations. What it does not supply: A general assurance metric or a known twofold safety multiplier.
  • Amodei, We Must Pace the Frontier, September 2026. What it supports: A proposal for evaluator access and coordination. What it does not supply: Proof of implemented, binding, reciprocal enforcement.

items.title: [AINews] Here are 6 Clones of Jev in 2 days
items.summary: We covered Jev’s launch on Wednesday , and they have completely taken over the timeline, with 36M views of their launch video (by comparison, OpenAI’s Navier Stokes result got 74M views, and Anthropic’s Fable 5 got 57M views) in just two days. It wasn’t open source 1 , so it invited tons of speculation and great demos and examples and salty schmidhubers and bad takes , which of course only fed the hype. Here’s a list. The best guesses are ModernBert and Diffusion: Laya : 421M params, ModernBERT -large encoder with two added transformer layers that score user-supplied options, PPO over sequence embeddings to output turn-by-turn conversion trajectories (probabilities from 0.0 to 1.0). salty that he did not get recognition; claims RLCD without justification confidence is entropy-based, not calibrated DiffusionGemmaJev: tackling this from a Diffusion model basis. Pretty close on benchmarks Bespoke Nimble : LoRA finetune of Qwen3.5-9B, using contrastive data curation. ( close but sllightly lower on benchmarks ) SemIf (fka OpenJev) ( HF ): 4B and 35B causal Qwen3.5 backbone with a tiny three-class NLI classifier on the last token. comparison vs Laya Jevlike : 40K byte embedding lightweight option-attention model. Each candidate becomes a query that reads from a shared context representation, then receives a score. Kev-0.5B : LoRA adapter + a small readout head on top of Qwen2.5-0.5B. Of course, not enough people are talking about the data side, which is acknowledged to be 100% synthetic . AI News for 9/17/2026-9/18/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Decision Models, Routing, and the “Jev” Wave Discriminative models broke out as a new systems primitive : The biggest technical conversation was around Jev , a non-generative decision model being positioned as a fast “ System 1 ” complement to LLMs. @ankrgyl said it is now available as an eval model in Braintrust with ~400x lower scoring cost versus prior setups, while @gabepereyra highlighted calibrated-probability use cases like routing, citation selection, escalation, and legal ops decisions. The more architectural take came from @hxiao , who argued Jev could pull tool calling, routing, and MCP-style decisions back from small generative LMs toward discriminative models; @signulll pushed the same idea further, framing this class as a near-zero-marginal-cost, on-device judgment layer for notifications, UI adaptation, and sensor-driven decisions. Open reproductions and ecosystem clones appeared immediately : @madiator released Bespoke Nimble , an “open Jev” recipe built from a LoRA fine-tune of Qwen3.5-9B using synthetic contrastive data curation and constrained decoding. On its curated eval, the base Qwen improved from 66% to 90% , versus 93% for Jev , with a reported 100ms on H100 and local usability. At the smaller end, @jaredpalmer released Kev-0.5B , a tiny Jev-like model based on Qwen2.5-0.5B that can run on a MacBook Pro. The reaction split roughly along prior experience: @MParakhin noted post-ChatGPT users treated it like a revelation, while pre-GPT ML people were more puzzled by the hype. The substantive question raised by @abacaj is the right one: a lot of demos emphasized speed more than quality , and there is still no standard benchmark for this category. The first compelling integrations were in browser/computer-use workflows : @levie demoed Jev classifying Box incident reports into escalation paths; @ndrezn showed browser use with LangChain + Jev and found it strong on tasks like the Wikipedia game and structured “folding laundry” workflows; @cline shipped a plugin giving Jev a browser in Cline. @hwchase17 explicitly called browser use the best Jev application he had seen so far. Net: this looks less like a chatbot story than a workflow control-plane story. Agent Tooling, Coding Harnesses, and Claude Code Standards AGENTS.md gained real momentum as a cross-tool convention : The highest-signal product update here was @trq212 announcing that Claude Code v2.1.277 now checks for AGENTS.md when no CLAUDE.md is present, with config-level toggle support. That effectively acknowledges AGENTS.md as an emerging standard rather than a one-tool convention, and @simonw immediately noted the practical payoff: fewer shim files that just point one format to the other. Harness design is becoming a first-class variable in coding-agent performance and cost : @pidotdev highlighted the Harness Tax analysis showing that a simple tool set— read, write, edit, bash —can reach the Pareto frontier on benchmark performance while reducing unnecessary spending. Relatedly, @_akhaliq pointed to the paper An Empirical Study of Harness Design for Coding Agents , underscoring that benchmark outcomes are increasingly shaped by harness structure , context setup, turn budgets, and tool affordances rather than just the base model. This is consistent with @dexhorthy ’s “software factory” argument that teams still need to read the code and deliberately design the human/agent interface. Model choice in software systems is bifurcating : Several practitioners described a split between “frontier for planning, cheap for execution.” @TheAhmadOsman summarized one stack as GPT 5.6 Sol XHigh for planning, GLM 5.3 Flash for implementation, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for other tasks. @kylebrussell reported an internal knowledge-base pipeline moving from Opus → Sonnet → GLM 5.2 → GLM 5.3 Flash , cutting spend by roughly two orders of magnitude since spring. Meanwhile @theo argued that in real-world coding the payoff from stronger models like Fable and Astra is not just code quality, but a subtler productivity gain in execution and iteration. Benchmarks, Recursive Self-Improvement, and Math Capability RSI discussion got more precise about what is actually “recursive” : @TheTuringPost offered a useful taxonomy: AI improving code or training methods is not, by itself, fully recursive if the surrounding improvement loop remains fixed. The key threshold is when AI can modify not just model internals, but search strategy, experience generation, research tooling, and the improvement process itself . That framing links well with @HuaxiuYaoML ’s RSI-Exam update, where GPT-6-astra remains #1 at 0.5126 , with Fable 5.1 entering at #2 with 0.4813 , and no model yet reaching the frontier-calibrated reference. Math benchmarks continued to fall to frontier models, but interpretation remains nuanced : @EpochAIResearch reported that another FrontierMath open problem was solved in an interactive session with GPT-6 Astra . Separately, @SAIRfoundation launched Open Math Model , pitching open models and tools for mathematics shaped by the research community. Against the “verifiability explains math strength” narrative, @steve47285 shared an argument that pretraining data , not merely verifiable reward structure, is the main reason LLMs are so good at math and coding. The meta-point from @sarahcat21 is worth keeping: we need not just better benchmarks, but better benchmark maintenance and audit tooling . Computer-use benchmarks are still far from saturation : @ValsAI launched CUA-Bench , testing real-time keyboard/mouse use across 6 games (with 3 kept private ) as a proxy for difficult human-easy tasks. Follow-up numbers from @ValsAI suggest this remains genuinely hard: all frontier models score below 20% . In parallel, @trycua open-sourced CUA-S1-FORMS , the first in a family of small “System One” computer-use models. The direction is notable: real-time action loops, video-grounded adaptation, and continuous learning, not just text-only planning. Infra, Training Systems, and Model Architecture Long-context and large-scale training infrastructure remain active optimization fronts : @Azaliamirh released Turbo-dLLM , an open-source library for training diffusion LLMs at scale, reporting 2.48x speedup at 512K context and 7.59x at 1M context on 8x H100s via Context-Sharded Block Parallelism . That aligns with practitioner attention on million-token regimes: @andrew_n_carr flagged a sharp quality increase in DeepSeek V4.1 Flash after context extension to 1M tokens , arguing that agents are context hungry . Architecture taxonomy debates are still alive : @ahatamiz1 argued that the field is overusing SSM as a label for any linear model. His proposal is to use linear RNNs as the umbrella term, with SSMs as one sub-family, distinguishing systems like Mamba2 from the GDN family on the basis that GDN behaves more like a gradient step on a local regression loss than a discretized ODE. For engineers tracking sequence-model alternatives to transformers, this is a useful nomenclature cleanup rather than mere pedantry. Edge/local neural program execution also got a notable update : @yuntiandeng described ProgramAsWeights , where developers specify an AI function in English, compile it once, and then run a small neural program locally on CPU with Wi‑Fi off . The code and models are public. This sits interestingly adjacent to the Jev conversation: both point toward smaller, specialized, locally runnable inference artifacts rather than ever-larger universal chat models. Robotics, Vision, Audio, and Generative Media Open robotics data releases were unusually substantive : @adamrasb announced the full ABC release, including code, 400+ hours of sim data on 24 tasks , and 5,850 labeled policy-evaluation episodes . In a more detailed companion post, @redstone_hong described ABC-130K as the largest open teleop dataset to date: 3,500 hours , 130K+ episodes , 195 tasks , collected on an $8K bimanual setup , with open hardware, training code, sim, and eval. The baseline science included sim-to-real correlation r = 0.91 on task progress and studies of offline metrics, scaling laws, and conditioning. Astra is showing up across evals and products, especially for vision : @skalskip92 reported GPT-6 Astra as the strongest vision model Roboflow has tested across detection, segmentation, box prompting, counting, reasoning, and video. The tradeoff remains material: a “high effort” setting improved detection from 82.1% to 83.6% mAP@50 but roughly doubled per-image cost from $0.050 to $0.101 and latency from 11s to 32s ( details ). Roboflow also integrated Astra into Auto Annotate. Speech and lip-sync saw strong benchmarked releases : @ArtificialAnlys reported Grok Voice Transcribe 2.0 reaching 2.7% WER on streaming final transcripts at 0.49s after end-of-speech, improving from 3.9% on its predecessor while keeping pricing at $0.20/hour streaming and $0.10/hour non-streaming . On the video side, @fal launched H3 Max Lip Sync , claiming #1 on both speed and quality in its evals with 11s median generation time , and @isidentical said the model was built by pushing diffusion RL into a verifiable lip-sync task. AI Safety, Evaluation Governance, and Security Anthropic’s evaluator-embedding strategy became more concrete—and more controversial : @AnthropicAI announced a partnership with Accenture on independent evaluation of frontier AI , saying the two organizations expect to invest at least $1B over five years to build capacity. This follows broader calls for embedded third-party evaluators with employee-level access. The reaction was mixed to hostile: critics questioned whether a consulting firm is the right vehicle for model red-teaming and safeguard assessment, while @TransluceAI emphasized that the conditions around independence and meaningful oversight are the real issue. The “rogue agents” / Hugging Face incident continued to drive debate about containment : @polynoamial clarified that his much-mocked thought experiment was about coordination between supposedly isolated agents , not weight exfiltration via thermal sensors, and argued the lesson from the HF incident is to avoid trusting sandbox isolation as a sole defense. @martin_casado made the strongest steelman: covert channels across air gaps are old, throughput can be tiny, and the real takeaway is layered defense rather than sensationalism. At the same time, @WSJ and @jeffjarvis pushed back on “rogue AI” framing entirely, arguing these events still reduce to human-configured systems doing what people enabled them to do . Policy pressure is building around safety laws and operational accountability : @TheRundownAI reported that California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order convening an expert panel to recommend stronger AI safety laws, including possible kill switches , embedded outside monitors, and required safety plans. Meanwhile, @sayashk pointed to a mismatch between rhetoric and incentives in AI security, criticizing OpenAI’s reported $6,500 bug bounty to a researcher who broke into an internal repo and disclosed it. The common theme across these posts is straightforward: independent oversight, layered defenses, and security incentives are moving from abstract governance talk into concrete operational design. This is consistent with @dexhorthy’s “software factory” argument that teams still need to read the code and deliberately design the human/agent interface.

  • Model choice in software systems is bifurcating: Several practitioners described a split between “frontier for planning, cheap for execution.” @TheAhmadOsman summarized one stack as GPT 5.6 Sol XHigh for planning, GLM 5.3 Flash for implementation, and DeepSeek V4.1 Flash for other tasks. @kylebrussell reported an internal knowledge-base pipeline moving from Opus → Sonnet → GLM 5.2 → GLM 5.3 Flash, cutting spend by roughly two orders of magnitude since spring. Meanwhile @theo argued that in real-world coding the payoff from stronger models like Fable and Astra is not just code quality, but a subtler productivity gain in execution and iteration.

Benchmarks, Recursive Self-Improvement, and Math Capability

  • RSI discussion got more precise about what is actually “recursive”: @TheTuringPost offered a useful taxonomy: AI improving code or training methods is not, by itself, fully recursive if the surrounding improvement loop remains fixed. The key threshold is when AI can modify not just model internals, but search strategy, experience generation, research tooling, and the improvement process itself. That framing links well with @HuaxiuYaoML’s RSI-Exam update, where GPT-6-astra remains #1 at 0.5126, with Fable 5.1 entering at #2 with 0.4813, and no model yet reaching the frontier-calibrated reference.

  • Math benchmarks continued to fall to frontier models, but interpretation remains nuanced: @EpochAIResearch reported that another FrontierMath open problem was solved in an interactive session with GPT-6 Astra. Separately, @SAIRfoundation launched Open Math Model, pitching open models and tools for mathematics shaped by the research community. Against the “verifiability explains math strength” narrative, @steve47285 shared an argument that pretraining data, not merely verifiable reward structure, is the main reason LLMs are so good at math and coding. The meta-point from @sarahcat21 is worth keeping: we need not just better benchmarks, but better benchmark maintenance and audit tooling.

  • Computer-use benchmarks are still far from saturation: @ValsAI launched CUA-Bench, testing real-time keyboard/mouse use across 6 games (with 3 kept private) as a proxy for difficult human-easy tasks. Follow-up numbers from @ValsAI suggest this remains genuinely hard: all frontier models score below 20%. In parallel, @trycua open-sourced CUA-S1-FORMS, the first in a family of small “System One” computer-use models. The direction is notable: real-time action loops, video-grounded adaptation, and continuous learning, not just text-only planning.

Infra, Training Systems, and Model Architecture

  • Long-context and large-scale training infrastructure remain active optimization fronts: @Azaliamirh released Turbo-dLLM, an open-source library for training diffusion LLMs at scale, reporting 2.48x speedup at 512K context and 7.59x at 1M context on 8x H100s via Context-Sharded Block Parallelism. That aligns with practitioner attention on million-token regimes: @andrew_n_carr flagged a sharp quality increase in DeepSeek V4.1 Flash after context extension to 1M tokens, arguing that agents are context hungry.

  • Architecture taxonomy debates are still alive: @ahatamiz1 argued that the field is overusing SSM as a label for any linear model. His proposal is to use linear RNNs as the umbrella term, with SSMs as one sub-family, distinguishing systems like Mamba2 from the GDN family on the basis that GDN behaves more like a gradient step on a local regression loss than a discretized ODE. For engineers tracking sequence-model alternatives to transformers, this is a useful nomenclature cleanup rather than mere pedantry.

  • Edge/local neural program execution also got a notable update: @yuntiandeng described ProgramAsWeights, where developers specify an AI function in English, compile it once, and then run a small neural program locally on CPU with Wi‑Fi off. The code and models are public. This sits interestingly adjacent to the Jev conversation: both point toward smaller, specialized, locally runnable inference artifacts rather than ever-larger universal chat models.

Robotics, Vision, Audio, and Generative Media

  • Open robotics data releases were unusually substantive: @adamrasb announced the full ABC release, including code, 400+ hours of sim data on 24 tasks, and 5,850 labeled policy-evaluation episodes. In a more detailed companion post, @redstone_hong described ABC-130K as the largest open teleop dataset to date: 3,500 hours, 130K+ episodes, 195 tasks, collected on an $8K bimanual setup, with open hardware, training code, sim, and eval. The baseline science included sim-to-real correlation r = 0.91 on task progress and studies of offline metrics, scaling laws, and conditioning.

  • Astra is showing up across evals and products, especially for vision: @skalskip92 reported GPT-6 Astra as the strongest vision model Roboflow has tested across detection, segmentation, box prompting, counting, reasoning, and video. The tradeoff remains material: a “high effort” setting improved detection from 82.1% to 83.6% mAP@50 but roughly doubled per-image cost from $0.050 to $0.101 and latency from 11s to 32s (details). Roboflow also integrated Astra into Auto Annotate.

  • Speech and lip-sync saw strong benchmarked releases: @ArtificialAnlys reported Grok Voice Transcribe 2.0 reaching 2.7% WER on streaming final transcripts at 0.49s after end-of-speech, improving from 3.9% on its predecessor while keeping pricing at $0.20/hour streaming and $0.10/hour non-streaming. On the video side, @fal launched H3 Max Lip Sync, claiming #1 on both speed and quality in its evals with 11s median generation time, and @isidentical said the model was built by pushing diffusion RL into a verifiable lip-sync task.

AI Safety, Evaluation Governance, and Security

  • Anthropic’s evaluator-embedding strategy became more concrete—and more controversial: @AnthropicAI announced a partnership with Accenture on independent evaluation of frontier AI, saying the two organizations expect to invest at least $1B over five years to build capacity. This follows broader calls for embedded third-party evaluators with employee-level access. The reaction was mixed to hostile: critics questioned whether a consulting firm is the right vehicle for model red-teaming and safeguard assessment, while @TransluceAI emphasized that the conditions around independence and meaningful oversight are the real issue.

  • The “rogue agents” / Hugging Face incident continued to drive debate about containment: @polynoamial clarified that his much-mocked thought experiment was about coordination between supposedly isolated agents, not weight exfiltration via thermal sensors, and argued the lesson from the HF incident is to avoid trusting sandbox isolation as a sole defense. @martin_casado made the strongest steelman: covert channels across air gaps are old, throughput can be tiny, and the real takeaway is layered defense rather than sensationalism. At the same time, @WSJ and @jeffjarvis pushed back on “rogue AI” framing entirely, arguing these events still reduce to human-configured systems doing what people enabled them to do.

  • Policy pressure is building around safety laws and operational accountability: @TheRundownAI reported that California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order convening an expert panel to recommend stronger AI safety laws, including possible kill switches, embedded outside monitors, and required safety plans. Meanwhile, @sayashk pointed to a mismatch between rhetoric and incentives in AI security, criticizing OpenAI’s reported $6,500 bug bounty to a researcher who broke into an internal repo and disclosed it. The common theme across these posts is straightforward: independent oversight, layered defenses, and security incentives are moving from abstract governance talk into concrete operational design.
